paragraphs.text: TIMOTHY TO THE CHURCH, IN FOUR BOOKS
BOOK I

1. Timothy, least of the servants of God, to the catholic Church spread throughout the whole world: grace to you and peace from God our Father and from Christ Jesus our Lord, with the Holy Spirit. Amen.

That most ancient and most foul serpent breathes many grave and deadly diseases of ruinous plague into you, with the bitter envy of his murderous jealousy and the hideous breath of his venomous mouth. Yet among them all I do not know whether any wastes you with a more bitter plague upon faithful souls, or stains your children more foully, than this: many of your people think it too little to brood in this life over the goods that God entrusted to them for holy use, bearing no fruit of mercy and kindness, unless they also carry their avarice, which is the servitude of idolatry, on into the times that come after death.

Perhaps you look around, and keep looking about, to see which of your people they are whom I am addressing. You need no long search to find them. All of them, I say, nearly all of them are what I am describing. For that outstanding and surpassing blessedness of your first people departed long ago. Then all who acknowledged Christ turned the perishable resources of worldly things into the everlasting wealth of heavenly possessions. They deprived themselves of the use of present things for the glorious hope of things to come, and bought immortal riches by embracing poverty here and now. And what now?

Now, in place of all these, avarice, greed and plunder have taken over, together with the vices that keep them company and are joined to them as if they were sisters: envy, enmities, cruelties, debauchery, unchastity and ruin. The resources that once served those higher ends now serve these vices. And so, I know not how, your good fortune fights against you yourself. Your vices have grown almost as much as your peoples, and discipline has withdrawn as much as abundance has come to you. Prosperity has brought profits, but they come with heavy interest in losses.

For as the peoples of the faith have multiplied, faith has diminished. As her children grow, the mother sickens. You, O Church, have grown weaker through the very increase of your fruitfulness. You slip back as you advance and become feebler as your forces grow. You have spread throughout the whole world members who bear the name of religion but lack its power. So you have begun to be rich in crowds and poor in faith. The richer you are in numbers, the poorer you are in devotion; your body has grown broader and your mind narrower. You are, so to speak, at once both greater and smaller than yourself, advancing and retreating in an almost new and unheard-of way, growing and shrinking at the same time.

For where now is that outstanding form of yours, and the beauty of your whole body? Where is that witness which the sacred writings bore to your living virtues: "Now the whole multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul, and no one said that any of the things he possessed was his own"? Of this you now have (oh grief and lamentation!) only the reading and not the virtue. You are present to it only in knowledge and absent from it in conscience.

For the greatest part of your children now trades in deadly wares. Like hucksters and innkeepers, they devote themselves to earthly markets, or rather hellish ones, which perish and destroy at once. They buy the loss of life with the gain of money. To acquire what is not theirs, they squander what is theirs. They entrust to the earth mournful treasures that will bring brief joy to their heirs and long grief to those who amassed them. They cheat both others and themselves of the use of present goods, and they hide infernal riches in deep caverns, burying their money and their hope together. This is exactly what our Lord's saying describes: "Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."

So they begrudge their own salvation. Their own souls are called to heaven, but they press them down to the earth with earthly weights. For the mind of one who hoards follows his treasure and is changed, as it were, into the nature of earthly matter, not only now but also in the future and forever. As it is written, life and death alike are set before a person, and he may stretch out his hand to whichever he wishes. So each person must possess in eternity what he has seized here, as it were with his own hand. Given over to his own will and choice, he will be bound in the future to the things he clung to here in his affections.

II. But some, no doubt, think themselves free of this offense because they do not keep their gold and wealth in the ground, though they keep it hidden away somewhere. Let no one deceive himself with ridiculous notions. Whoever serves earthly greed by increasing his wealth is always burying gold in the earth. This is what the Savior teaches in the Gospel when he says, "Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth," and again, "but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven." These words cannot be understood in a carnal sense. Do all the wicked place their material treasures in the earth, or all the good in heaven? Certainly not.

So the force of the sacred utterance expressed the effects and powers of spiritual realities. Earthly and hellish things are owed to greed and avarice, but heavenly and eternal things to mercy and generosity. That is why the distinction between earthly and heavenly treasure was drawn: those who stored up for greed and avarice would know that they were placing their wealth in hell, while those who stored up for mercy and kindness would rejoice that they were preparing heavenly treasures. So he named the places where treasures lie according to the merits of those who store them. The treasures are said to be already where those who store them will one day be.

III. But perhaps it may seem a harsh judgment that calls everyone equally to perfection and binds all by a single law, since the condition of all is certainly not the same. One could quite rightly reply that since everyone wants to live forever, everyone ought to act so as to share in that life. It is utterly ill-advised and foolish for some to act in such a way that what they want in their desires and prayers, they seem not to want in fact and deed.

Yet let us consider especially that part of Christians, that is, of your children, which is held back from perfection by certain hindrances and by family ties that it thinks cannot be broken. First in this group, I think, are those who plead that concern for their offspring, and a sort of overpowering love for their children, drive them to seek money and enlarge their wealth as widely as possible. As if anyone who is a father neither could nor should be anything at all but rich, and could not love his children without multiplying his wealth! Or as if avarice and greed were the strength and marrow of affection, because, as they suppose, love can no more exist without greed than a body without marrow.

If that is so, then without doubt parental piety is wholly a cause of evil, and it contains not feelings of good affection but incitements to vice. Where, then, is that sacred oracle of divine authority: "Piety is profitable for all things"? On this view it would not only fail to be profitable for all things, but would be harmful in nearly all. If it is the begetter of greed, it contains far more evil than good, according to that saying of holy Scripture:

"Greed is the root of all evils." So if greed is the root of all evils, and it is conceived in the womb of piety and nourished, as it were, on its poisonous milk, then we should blame not so much greed, which is born of piety as its parent, as piety itself, which produces such a daughter. It follows that if piety is so pestilent and so harmful, it is best neither to love nor to be loved. Parents ought not to seek a love that harms themselves, and children ought not to desire one that will injure their parents.

Yet that love brings sickness not only to parents but also to children. It is grievous both to those who give birth to ruinous inheritances and to those who are raised as wicked heirs amid the most wicked gain. Hence nearly all children succeed their parents in their vices as much as in their estates, and take on their fathers' depravity as much as their wealth. Always taking on their fathers' ways, they begin to possess their fathers' wickedness before their property. For they possess their parents' goods only once the parents are dead, but they possess their character while the parents are still alive and well. So before they begin to own their fathers' property, they already hold their fathers in their souls. Before they have the things that are falsely called goods, they have the things that are shown to be truly evils.

IV. What then? Since this is so, do I perhaps seem to forbid parents to feel affection for their children? Not at all. What could be so savage, so inhuman, so contrary to the law, as for us to say that children are not to be loved, when we confess that even enemies are to be loved? Or for us to forbid the affection that nature supplies, when we bestow even the affection that nature forbids? Or for us to wrench from the mind the love it has, when we try even to plant in it the love it does not have?

It is not so. We say not only that children are to be loved, but that they are to be loved especially and above all things, and that nothing at all is to be preferred to them except God alone. For this too is what it means to love them especially: to put before one's children him whom it is in no way good to put after them. What, then, do we mean when we say children are to be loved, and how are they to be loved? How else, without doubt, than as God himself has laid down? There is no better love of children than the love taught by the one who gave the children themselves. Nor can one's offspring be better loved than when they are loved in him by whom they were given. How, then, did God command children to be loved?

I do not say it myself; let the divine word itself say it. It speaks to all fathers in general: "that they should hand on the commandments of God to their children, so that they might set their hope in God and not forget the works of their God, and might seek out his commandments." And elsewhere: "And you fathers," it says, "do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and correction of the Lord."

You see what wealth God bids parents provide for their children. He does not mean treasures of money, nor sacks heavy with gold, which carry much weight but even more iniquity. Nor does he mean proud houses towering over lofty cities, roofs raised beyond human sight, or pinnacles thrust into the clouds where the occupant lives in the air. Nor, finally, does he mean boundless estates, too large for their owner to know, which think it beneath them to endure partners and count having neighbors an injury.

God, then, does not command these things, nor does he stretch the care of fatherly love into the slavish duties of managing earthly affairs. He commands few things, but they bring salvation. They are easy but holy, sparing as precepts but great in fruit, brief in writing but everlasting in blessedness. "Parents," he says, "do not provoke your children to indignation, but bring them up in the discipline and correction of the Lord," that is, as the prophet said, "so that they might set their hope in God and not forget the works of their God, and might seek out his commandments."

See what riches God loves, what wealth he requires to be laid up for our children, what resources he commands to be provided: faith and the fear of God, modesty, holiness and discipline. They are not earthly, cheap, perishing or fleeting; they are glorious indeed. Since he is the God of the living and not of the dead, he rightly commanded that children be given the things through which they might live forever, not the things through which they would die for all eternity. No one doubts that for nearly all the wicked and unbelieving, worldly riches are a cause of death rather than of life. As God says, "How hard it will be for those who have money to enter the kingdom of heaven!" And again: "It is easier," he says, "for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven." Hence also his specific command: "Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven."

The passages quoted earlier and now show two kinds of treasure: one that fathers store up for their children, and another that they store up for themselves. How for their children? By instructing them in their duty to God and in the fear of God. How for themselves? By storing up treasures for themselves in heaven. This is wonderfully arranged. Money perishes but discipline is immortal, and nearly all parents love their children more than themselves. So they keep the perishable goods for themselves and give the everlasting goods to their children. In this way they look after both their love and their salvation, gaining a twofold and immortal good. Through things eternal they make their children eternal, and to win blessedness for themselves they use good works to turn what is by nature perishable into things eternal. Why, then, are you so agitated, fatherly love?

Why do you strain yourself to acquire earthly and perishing things? You can give your children nothing greater than a good, received through you, that they will never wholly lose. So there is no need to hoard earthly treasures for your son. Nothing will make him richer than making your son himself a treasure of God.

V. Although all this is so, and is true and most beneficial, I do not mean that I would wholly exclude children from their fathers' goods and property. But we will discuss this later. Meanwhile, some people think they will not be guilty even if they do not give their wealth to honor the Gospel, to secure their own salvation, or to any service of God. Instead, out of caprice and unbelief, and with impious and pagan vanity, they make it over to any heirs at all, irreligious or wealthy. So let us see briefly by whom these resources were given and for what purpose. Once we have shown both who gave them and why, we can more easily prove to whom they should be returned and to what use they should be put.

No one, I think, who deserves to be counted among human beings at all, doubts that all the wealth of this world is given to everyone as a divine gift. Unless, perhaps, someone is so wise that he believes the world itself was given by God to the human race, but the things in the world were not given to people by God! So if God has granted all things to all people, no one can doubt that what we have received as God's gift we ought to return to the worship of God, and that what we have taken from his generosity we ought to spend on his work.

For this is what it means to acknowledge God's gift and use his benefits well: to honor with his gifts the one from whom you received them. Even examples from human affairs teach this. Suppose one person, out of kindness and generosity, granted another the use of certain property. Suppose the second person forgot the one through whom he had gained its enjoyment and tried to take the ownership of what was lent away from him and transfer it to others. Would he not be judged the most ungrateful and faithless of all? He would have forgotten a kind and most generous man and tried to strip him of his rights of ownership, the very man who had enriched him with the use of that property.

In the same way, we have received only the use of the things we hold. We use resources lent to us by God, and we are, as it were, tenants who hold at the owner's pleasure. In the end, when we leave this world, we leave everything here whether we like it or not. Since we hold only the use and enjoyment of these things, why do we try to take what we cannot carry with us away from the Lord's ownership and transfer it to others? Why do we not use in good faith the little things God has given us? We held them as long as we were allowed, as long as the one who lent them permitted.

What could be more right or more honorable than that, when property leaves the one who had its use, possession should return to the one who granted that use? Indeed, the very words of God, spoken through the sacred Scriptures, command this, saying to each of us: "Honor the Lord with your substance." And elsewhere he says, "Pay your debt." How kind and indulgent is the Lord our God, inviting us to give away the resources of our earthly substance! "Honor the Lord," he says, "with your substance." Although everything we have received from him is his, he says it is ours so that we may give it. He calls the possession ours so that the doer's reward may be greater. A giver necessarily reaps more fruit when the gift appears to come from what is his own.

VI. Yet in case the human mind grew arrogant because the Lord had called this substance ours, he added, "Pay your debt." Those whom devotion did not entice to give, necessity would compel to pay; those whom their own faith did not draw to holy work, necessity would at least constrain. First he says, "Honor the Lord with your substance"; then he says, "Pay your debt." That is to say: if you are devout, give it as your own; if you are not devout, pay it back as not your own. So he rightly set down both the willingness to give and the necessity of paying.

This certainly amounts to saying to everyone: you are both urged by exhortation and bound by demand to holy work. Give if you are willing; pay if you are not. The apostle too gives this same warning when he commands the rich not to be haughty and not to hope in uncertain riches but in the living God, "who provides us," he says, "with all things to enjoy, for the purpose of good works." In one saying he taught both who gives riches and why he gives them.

By saying that hope is to be placed in God, who provides all things, he showed that people are made rich by God. By adding "for the purpose of good works," he teaches that what he said God grants is provided only for the sake of good works: "He provides all things," he says, "for the purpose of good works." That is, God makes people wealthy in substance so that they may be rich in good works. He wants them to exchange the riches they have received, and by investing those resources in good works and using them well, to make everlasting the wealth of God that they hold for a time in this world. So, acknowledging the gifts of God, they may rejoice in a twofold good: those who are rich in this world may deserve to be rich in heaven as well.

VII. This, then, is how riches are to be acquired, sought, kept and increased. Otherwise it is an incalculable evil not to use well the goods God has given. "Nothing," says holy Scripture, "is more wicked than a miser," and "riches kept to their owner's harm" are the worst and deadliest kind of sickness. It is true. For what is worse or more wretched than to turn present goods into future evils? God gave these things so that everlasting blessedness of life might be gained from them, and yet some use these very things to seek death and eternal damnation.

Here we should also consider this: if riches that are kept are kept to a person's harm, how much greater the harm when they are heaped up! How few of the rich now have such restraint that they are content to guard their wealth and no longer wish to add to it! O the misery of our times and of the church's people: to what have they been reduced! Scripture says that keeping wealth is a kind of great crime, yet now merely not increasing it is thought a kind of virtue.

So, as we said above, how can some think themselves not guilty at all if they have not provided for themselves even at death by distributing their wealth? They are guilty already for keeping everything until death. Or how will those not be guilty who, with utterly faithless vanity, have handed over their resources to just anyone? Even those who did not deprive themselves of some portion of their property in this life for the honor of God will be guilty. Our Lord shows this very thing through the apostle, saying: "Come now, you rich, weep and wail over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure in the last days."

There is a severity in these divine words that lies hidden in mystery, much greater and more terrible. But apart from that, I think what lies plain on the surface is enough to fill everyone with fear and trembling. He speaks specifically to the rich. He commands them to wail, announces evils to come and threatens everlasting fire. What makes these threats all the more fearful is their cause. It is not murder, fornication or sacrilegious impiety, nor any of the other vices that slaughter souls with a deadly sword and everlasting death. It is wealth alone, insane greed, the hunger for gold and silver. He wanted to show that these are enough for a person's eternal damnation even if there were no other guilt. What could be said more simply or more plainly?

He does not say to the rich man: "You are to be tormented because you are a murderer," or "You are to be tormented because you are a fornicator." He says only: "You are to be tormented because you are rich," that is, because you use your riches badly and do not understand that they were given to you for holy work. Riches are not harmful in themselves; the minds of those who misuse them are guilty. Wealth itself is not what brings punishment on a person. The rich make their wealth into their own punishment, because by refusing to use their riches well they turn those very riches into torments for themselves. "You have stored up treasure," he says, "in the last days."

He spoke well: having said "you have stored up treasure," he added "in the last days." This was to make the guilt of those who store up greater, since even the very end of the age made their treasures more odious. "You have stored up treasure," he says, "in the last days." The treasures accuse them of greed, and the last days accuse them of unbelief. So there is a double offense, of greed and of unbelief. God says, "You shall not covet," so it was certainly a crime to covet treasures at any other time. But to heap them up even at the end of the world is without doubt a greater crime, because of the unbelief it shows.

VIII. Someone may have judged my discourse so far to be harsh. And it truly is harsh, if I have urged anything that is not grounded in the authority of the sacred testimonies. Let it be thought harsh, if it has said anything as severe as what the apostle preached here. And I have not even added the saying of our Lord in which he declared that all who had not renounced everything they possessed were entirely unworthy of him.

Since this is so, is it not right, I ask, to judge what we have said as most indulgent and most gentle? For people to whom we cannot give perfect health, we at least look for some help toward a salvation already despaired of, and where we cannot heal their life, we try to ease their death. What, after all, is perfect health? What but to live well in this life? What is the last treatment? What but to provide good provisions for the journey, if only at the very end? What is perfect health? What but to use well the things God has entrusted to us? What is the final remedy? What but at least afterwards to do what you are sorry you did not do before?

Someone thinks what I say is harsh. Let it be judged harsh, plainly harsh, unless it is such that, compared with the apostle's severity, it seems mild and lenient. For the apostle calls the rich to lamentation; we call them to a remedy. The apostle calls riches fire; we wish to make of riches waters that put out the fire, according to the saying: As water quenches fire, so almsgiving quenches sin.

The apostle testifies that damnation lies in riches wrongly hoarded; I wish that out of what he calls eternal death all may purchase everlasting life. I do not, of course, think it enough for eternal life that someone entangled in carnal vices, after growing old in shameful deeds right up to death, should dispose of everything well at his passing, unless he has first renounced his sins, thrown off that filthy, mud-stained tunic of crimes, and received the new garment of conversion and holiness from the hand of the apostle who preaches it.

Otherwise a man does not stop sinning if, placed at the end, it is only impossibility and not his will that makes him withdraw from his crimes. For one who departs from evil deeds only through death does not leave his crimes; rather his crimes leave him. Thus, though shut out from vices by necessity, he is still sinning, I think, even when they have ceased, because in his mind he has not yet stopped, since he would still wish to sin if he could. So a man rests on no good hopes who sins in life precisely so as to buy off the mass of his sins at death, and thinks he will escape not because he is good but because he is rich.

As if God sought not people's lives but their money, and wished to accept from all who do evil in the hope of buying off their misdeeds nothing but coins for their crimes, and, like corrupt judges, demanded silver in order to sell sins!

It is not so. Giving is certainly of very great benefit, but not to those who live wickedly in the hope of a final act of giving to come, who commit crimes trusting that they can buy impunity. It benefits rather those who, deceived by the slipperiness of youth, or the cloud of error, or the fault of ignorance, or finally by a lapse of human frailty, at last begin to come to their senses, as if after the deathly crisis of a very grave illness, or after the grief of a disturbed mind. As the insane return to their senses after their frenzy, so these return after their error, differing from them in one thing only: the former rejoice after they have escaped their sickness, these lament after they have received their health.

And not without reason. The former rejoice the more, the more fully they feel they have recovered their health; these are the more ashamed, the more clearly they recognize the disease of their error. So the former must exult and these must mourn, because the former blame their sickness on their constitution, while these blame their straying on themselves; and so the former are glad about the remedy, and these anxious about their guilt.

IX. I therefore admonish everyone, but especially those whom the terror of grave offenses torments, and in whom an unhappier conscience sighs at the memory of sins that deserve punishment: first, though they have fallen, let them not linger in their fall or roll about in their wallows like filthy swine, which, once they have plunged their heated bellies into the mire, never satisfy their filthy pleasure until they have rolled every limb completely in the mud. Let them not follow the natural filthiness of these animals, nor settle into falls that wickedly flatter them, nor linger in the abyss of lusts and bury themselves in their own ruins. Rather, let them rise at once where they fell, and think of getting up even as they fall; and if by swift repentance it can be done in any way, let the remedy of the one rising again be so quick that scarcely a trace of the fall can be seen.

In such cases, then, this is the first work of healing: that the sick shudder at their diseases, that the injured hurry to treat their wounds, and that the wounded at once pull the arrows from their bodies. A poultice or a clasp is best applied while the wounds are still warm, and the flesh of a wound knits together more quickly when it is not left gaping for long. For an ulcer in the body spreads if it festers, and if canker follows a wound, death must follow the canker.

So sinners must first of all flee these evils and give no place to the devil, lest he who pushed them into ruin while they stood should hurl them, once fallen, into death. But if the force of the disease or the carelessness of the sick is so great that they drag their decaying health on to their last days, I do not know what to say; I have no idea at all what to promise. To call those in danger away from seeking a last remedy is harsh and impious; yet to promise anything from so late a cure is rash.

Yet it is undoubtedly better that hands withered by paralysis, however long, should still be raised to heaven with some effort than that they should be dissolved in deadly despair. It is better to leave nothing untried than to give the dying no care at all, especially since, though I do not know whether attempting something at the very end is a medicine, attempting nothing is certainly perdition. And one thing I do know: whoever has brought the miseries of a long sickness to this extremity owes, beyond all words, a vast lamentation for his errors, having never recognized his errors.

X. And what will happen meanwhile? When will he mourn who has lost the days for mourning? When will he make satisfaction who has let the time for satisfaction slip away? He will flee, no doubt, to long fasts. That is indeed something, if it is joined with almsgiving, according to the saying: Fasting with almsgiving is good. But how will a lengthy confession help one who is already at the end? He will wear down his flesh with sackcloth and befoul it with ashes and cinders, so that the hardships of present austerities may make up for the softness of past pleasure, and he may pay off the guilt of long luxuries through the service of a self-inflicted suffering that pleads his cause. But when will he do such great things, when, with his end already near, he is shut out even from doing modest ones?

Then the severity of faith, acting as judge, will subject the guilty man in his own body to the crosses of various afflictions, so that by eagerly seeking present punishment he may merit the indulgence of eternal absolution. But when the body is already failing, where will the mind, as censor, exercise its office of strictness? For a judge cannot exercise the discretion of severity when the accused can no longer bear to be tried.

There is one thing, then, that, with all aids and supports taken away, can help one who is tottering and forsaken: let him take refuge in that holy and wholesome counsel of the most blessed Daniel, who, wishing to heal the Babylonian king of the sores contracted through offending God, compounded a poultice out of mercy, saying: Therefore, O king, let my counsel please you: redeem your sins with mercies and your iniquities with compassion on the poor; perhaps the Lord will be patient with your offenses. So let this man do as Daniel said.

Let him use the medicine offered to another for his own wounds; let him fear the example of disobedient obstinacy; let him consider what he himself will suffer in death, when he sees what the Assyrian king endured in life. It is a plain lesson about pride and rebellion. Let him consider whether he himself, if he does not listen, will escape once he is dead, when he sees that that king, who did not listen, lost himself while still alive. Let him offer, then, even as he dies, to free his soul from everlasting punishments, at least his property, since he can do nothing else now. But let him offer it with compunction, with tears; let him offer it with sorrow, with grief.

Otherwise offerings do no good, for they please not by their price but by the disposition behind them. The giver's mind is not commended by the gifts, but the gifts by the mind; money does not commend faith, but faith commends money. So whoever wishes what he offers to God to benefit him, let him offer in this way. For man does God no favor in what he gives; rather God does man a favor in what he accepts, since even what man has is the gift of God, his Lord. Thus in what man offers, man does not give back what is his own; the Lord receives back what is his.

So when anyone offers his means to God, let him offer them not with the presumption of a donor but with the humility of a debtor paying what he owes. Let him not believe that he is discharging his sins, but that he is lightening them; let him offer not with confidence of redemption but in the duty of supplication; not as one repaying the whole debt, but as one wishing to repay at least a little of a great one. For even if he hands over all he has, as far as his possessions go, he does not pay what he owes, as measured by the greatness of his sins. And therefore, though he offers, let him pray God that his offering may be pleasing, lamenting the very fact that he offers late, lamenting and repenting that he did not do so sooner. So it will come about, as the prophet says, that God may perhaps be merciful to your offenses.

XI. But someone says, “Is he then to offer God everything he has?” Let him not offer everything he has, if he does not think he owes everything he has. I do not ask whose it is that is offered, or from whom what is given back was first received; I say only this: let him not offer everything as a debt, if he does not think he owes everything for his guilt. “Is he then to offer everything?” asks someone, sinner though he is. No: nothing, if not with faith; nothing, if not with eagerness; nothing, if not with prayer; nothing, unless in this spirit: that he counts among God's chief benefits the very fact that God gave him the will to offer, and judges that more is bestowed on him in what he leaves to God than in what he had before. For what a person possesses is temporary, but what is left to God is everlasting.

“Everything?” someone says. But I say that this everything is too little. For what then? Does anyone already know whether his offerings make up for the measure of his sins? Does anyone already know whether there is as much in the act of appeasement as there is gravity in the offense? If any sinner knows at what price he can redeem his offenses, let him use that knowledge for his redemption. But if he does not know, why should he not offer as much as he can? Then, if he cannot make up for his sins by the size of the price, he may at least make up for them by the devotion of his mind. For he shows the perfect fruit of conscience who leaves nothing held back within his conscience.

Some no doubt complain that these things are harsh and immoderate, especially since the prophet we spoke of seems to have admonished the Babylonian king only to give much, not to sell off everything. For the moment I do not bring forward the testimonies of the gospel or take refuge in the voice of God speaking; I do not argue that one thing was commanded by the old law and another by the new. That is why the apostle says, Behold, the old things have passed away; all things have become new, and all things are from God. By these words he teaches that we must do not the old things according to the letter but the new things according to God.

For now I am content with what the prophet alone said. He was speaking to a king, and not the king of a single city but, as it then seemed, of the whole world, who certainly could not hand over by will to the needy the peoples he ruled, or give barbarian nations to the poor like coins, or turn kingdoms spread far and wide into alms for the poor. So the prophet says, “Redeem your sins with mercies,” that is: give gold to the needy, since you cannot give a kingdom; distribute your wealth, since you cannot pass on your power. And so he seems to have commanded him to give everything, since the only thing he did not command him to distribute was what he could not pay out.

XII. Perhaps we are exaggerating the matter in words and raising it too high. Let us see, then, what it really is. Redeem your sins, he says, with mercies. What is it to redeem something? To pay, I suppose, the price of the things redeemed. I do not ask what that king's sins were; let him know how much he ought to have paid to redeem what he did. It is you I address, whose case this is; it is you I call upon, whose peril is at stake. Do what the prophet said: Redeem your sins with mercies. Do not leave God everything you have, if you do not think everything you have is needed for your sins.

Assess most carefully the faults you have committed; assess the various kinds of your sins. See what you owe for lies, what for curses and perjuries, what for carelessness in your thoughts, what for impurity of speech, what, finally, for every impulse of an evil will. Add lastly, if any of them weigh on your conscience, those of which the apostle speaks: adulteries, fornications, lewdness, drunkenness, impurity hateful to God, avarice the handmaid of idolatry; and after these perhaps also crimes incurred by shedding human blood.

When you have counted them all up, weigh the price of each. And after that I do not ask you to hand over to God everything you have for your sins: only pay what you owe. But I add, after all this, that when you have considered and assessed your offenses, you will owe all the more for your evils the more cheaply you value your sins, since, as the apostle says, whoever thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself. I need not mention that that king, who still had his life before him and was perhaps young, was nonetheless commanded to hasten to redeem his sins; but you owe so much the more on your own account, because you are doing this either as you die or when you are about to die at any moment.

Great indeed must be the generosity and devotion that can make up for the fact that you give these things back to your Lord only when you can no longer keep them yourself. All the more so since to all this is added that the prophet himself, who calls that king to redeem his crimes, by the very things he says must be done shows him not so much the security of pardon as a way of seeking salvation. For when he says, Redeem your sins with mercies, and perhaps God will be merciful to your offenses, the very word “perhaps” points to a hope; it does not promise certainty.

From this one can understand how hard it is for sinners already at their last to attain full pardon by any generosity whatever, since the prophet himself, who urges that God's mercy be sought, nevertheless did not dare to promise that it would be won. He gives counsel about the act and yet is doubtful of the result; he makes himself one who urges the doing, not one who guarantees the obtaining. Why so? Because all sinners must try everything on their own behalf, even at the last, though they can presume nothing. For if the prophet does not promise that king full pardon through the generous giving of good works alone, the sinner who has not done penance for his errors can understand how great and how lavish a generosity he needs at the last, if he wishes to obtain from the Lord by a late devotion what he cannot claim by law.
BOOK II.

I. We have spoken of the remedies for sins, or rather of the hopes and consolations of remedies. The first aid in seeking salvation is for the sinner to repent of his error. Next, as the sacred word says, he should at once redeem his sins by works of mercy. Finally, if he has not done this, he should at least leave nothing untried when he is dying, so that he may help himself even by a last offering of his property. But perhaps someone will reply: if sinful men are bound by this need to redeem their crimes, then the saints, who are free of crimes, are surely not bound by it. They therefore have no reason to give away their substance, since they have nothing that they must redeem by generosity. I hear this; but what it amounts to we shall soon see.

Meanwhile, even if there are no past evils that a holy man must redeem with all his possessions, there are still everlasting goods that he ought to buy at a great price. But more on this later. For now I say this freely and affirm it firmly: there is not a single one of the saints who is not in debt to God in many things. Therefore whatever he gives to his Lord, he is not so much giving as paying back.

First, to speak of the general benefits: whoever you are, whether one of the saints or one of the rich, it was first by God's goodwill and gift that you were born, nourished and brought up. By his gift you were supplied with what is necessary for life and enriched even with what is not necessary. Your Lord granted you more for your use than the measure of use required. In short, he extended his gifts beyond your hopes, and, what is greatest and rarest, his gifts surpassed even your prayers.

After all this I add that the same Lord who first brought you into being by his gift afterwards saved you by his passion as well. For your sake, O man, who are earth and clay, or rather a tiny portion of earth and clay, the Lord of all things came to earth. He came forth from flesh and in flesh alike, humbled even to the shame of human birth, the filth of swaddling clothes and the lowliness of the manger. He endured the sufferings of this life, which were unworthy of him: the wearisome round of eating and drinking, of sleeping and waking, and the humiliating necessities of this perishable existence. He endured, finally, the foul company of the men who lived around him: crowds smeared with the mud of filthy sins, always guilty of the misdeeds of an evil conscience, breathing out the stench of their shameful deeds. They were therefore unable to receive heavenly precepts or to bear the radiance of that holy brightness, because the splendor of divine light overwhelmed eyes darkened by sin.

And not only this. After all these things, add the insolent opposition of a proud people. Add the insults, add the curses, the impious persecution, the false testimony, the bloody sentence, the mockery of the crowd, the spitting, the scourging: most bitter punishments indeed, but indignities more bitter than the punishments. Add the crown of thorns, the cup of vinegar, the food of gall: the Lord of all condemned by men, the salvation of the human race hanging on the gibbet, God dying under the law of the earthly condition.

II. Since this is so, whoever you are who either are holy or believe yourself holy, tell me, I ask you: can even these things alone be repaid, even if nothing else were owed? Whatever a man may endure for God, what God suffered for man can never be repaid. Even if the suffering itself is no different in the kind of punishment, it must be vastly different because of the difference between those who suffer. But perhaps you say that what we have described is a debt shared by all men, and that the whole human race is liable for it without distinction. That is true.

But does anyone owe less because someone else owes the same? If a hundred men had signed bonds for a hundred sesterces each, would one man's debt be lightened because all are debtors for the same sum? For each one, says the apostle, will bear his own burden, and each will give account for himself. In no way, then, is one man's load lightened by another's, nor is a defendant acquitted because he has many companions. Nor is a dreadful condemnation any lighter for anyone because the condemned man appears to have many partners in his punishment.

So the debt I spoke of above, though general, is undoubtedly also particular. Though common to all, it belongs in a special way to each. It reaches all equally, yet nothing is taken off the total for any one person. For just as Christ suffered for all, so he suffered for each. He spent himself equally for all and for each, and gave himself wholly to all and wholly to each. Therefore, whatever the Savior bestowed by his passion, all together owe him the whole of it and each person owes him the whole of it. Indeed each person owes almost more than all together, because each has received as much as all. When one person receives what all receive, the favor is more remarkable even if the measure is equal. So even though he receives the same thing, he seems to owe more, because a single person is more deeply indebted when he is treated on a level with everyone. So much for this, since some of the saints do not think themselves in debt to God, because they cannot reckon the size of the debt.

III. But perhaps someone will say, not that the saints are not debtors, but that worldly men, who have more sins, have much greater debts. That is as if someone were to say: I am innocent because another is more guilty; I am just because another is unjust; I am exceedingly good because another is exceptionally wicked. In the first place, it does not become a holy mind to think that its own goods increase through the evils of others, or to consider itself better by comparing itself with worse men. It is the most wretched kind of consolation to take comfort from the miseries of sinners. The apostle bids us rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep, and bids each of us look not to his own interests but to those of others.

But grant that such a comparison seems just and honorable. Can it also be thought reliable? Who can be sure enough about that great and terrible future judgment of God? Who can say: I owe less, he owes more? Who, finally, can presume about himself or despair of someone else? For we shall all, says the apostle, stand before the judgment seat of Christ, and

each one will bear his own burden. “Is there no difference, then,” someone asks, “between saints and sinners?” Clearly there is a great one, almost beyond measure. But Scripture says, Blessed is the man who is always fearful, and the mind of the wise is never secure about its own salvation. So although there is a great difference between saints and sinners, I still ask all who profess religion: who, by his own conscience, is holy enough to satisfy himself? Who does not tremble at the dreadful severity of that future examination? Who is secure about his everlasting safety?

And if no one is, as indeed no one should be, let any man tell me, I beg you: why does he not strive with all the strength of his substance to redeem, at least by a devout act at his death, whatever he incurred by offending in his life? Yet I want all my readers to know that in saying this I am not speaking of all the saints. I mean only those who have professed religion and still do not give up their riches.

For there is nothing to be said about those who have freed themselves of all baggage to follow the Savior's way, and who purchase Christ, the Lord of the law, not by holiness alone but also by poverty. There is nothing to say except what the prophet also said: But to me your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored. I honor all of these as nothing less than imitators of Christ, I revere them as nothing less than images of Christ, and I look up to them as nothing less than members of Christ. I mention them only so that I may become worthy of remembering them.

IV. But perhaps what we said above may seem insulting to those who profess the religious life. “What then,” someone asks, “if a widow is rich, yet keeps her widowhood amid a great abundance of wealth? What if a virgin has professed integrity and is devoted to the holiness of an undefiled body? What if a married couple live without marital relations, each denying himself to the other, having as though not having? What if a monk has served as God's soldier from the cradle? What if a cleric carries out the service of the sacred ministry with faithful devotion? Are even these in danger of losing the fruit of eternal salvation if they keep their wealth intact while they live, or do not leave it to the needy when they die?”

My words and authority are too slight to pronounce a verdict on a question of this kind. Let us see, then, what the tongues of the sacred books and the voices of the heavenly commandments proclaim about all these things. Then we shall most rightly shape our own opinion by the standard God has given. First of all, no one should now think he can take refuge in the comfort of ancient examples and say that some saints, perhaps, were rich either under the law or before the law. That time has passed; the principle has changed. Before the law, everyone was free to choose whether to keep wealth or

even to pursue it, since the rod of heavenly prohibitions did not yet chastise anyone. For where there is no law, says the apostle, there is no transgression either. So it was the law that made something unlawful: for I would not have known covetousness, says the apostle, if the law had not said, You shall not covet.

And so man freely possessed wealth, which God had not censured before the law. Under the law, too, almost the same right was available to everyone, since the law did not forbid a man to have whatever he wished, provided he had it justly. So in those days all the saints without exception used all their possessions within the limits the law prescribed, walking, as we read, blameless in all the commandments and ordinances of God.

So indeed walked those of whom these things are recorded. There was the prophetess Anna, living in fasting and prayer. There was that Nathanael of whom we read, exalted by being praised as a true Israelite and made admirable by the testimony of the Lord and God himself. There was Tobit, who went beyond the precepts of the law in the greatness of his devotion. He served by burying the dead even at the risk of death, and he provided for the needy to the point of being in need himself. He came to such a pitch of generosity that he assigned to his hired man a share of all his goods. What may be more wonderful, he did this when he was already rich, and, more wonderful still, when he had become rich after being poor, since wealth that follows poverty usually stirs up a greater desire for possessions.

V. Such, then, were the saints of that time: they had everything according to the law and gave up everything according to the law. Everyone who obeyed the law was perfect. A man under the law who did less back then was as devout as a man under the gospel who does more now, for in those days the law was, as it were, the gospel. Hence whoever showed himself obedient to the law at that time had, as it were, fulfilled the gospel. So no one should now think he can take refuge in the law; for, as the apostle says, the old things have passed away and all things have become new.

In those days there was more indulgence and more license. Then the eating of meat was commended; now abstinence is. Then there were very few days of fasting in a whole lifetime; now the whole of life is like one fast. Then vengeance was available to the injured; now patience is required. Then the law served the angry; now it opposes them. Then it held out a sword to the accuser; now it holds out charity. Then the law indulged even the allurements of the flesh; now the gospel does not indulge even a glance. Then bodily pleasures had a certain license; now even the eyes are ordered to keep strict watch over themselves. Then the law widened one husband's bed to take in many wives; now, through the devotion of chaste affection, it constrains a man even to the point of excluding the one.

For it remains, says the apostle, that those who have wives should be as though they had none, those who weep as though not weeping, those who rejoice as though not rejoicing, those who buy as though not possessing, and those who use this world as though not using it; for the form of this world is passing away. See how briefly the teacher sent by God has regulated everything and enclosed it all within a single perfection, not only forbidding what is unlawful but also restricting what is lawful. He cuts back the use of marriage, faithless weeping, intemperate joy, the lust for having, the desire for buying, and finally the brief and shadowy pleasure of this world itself. And why all this?

Why, surely, except because, as he himself said, the form of this world is passing away? How far, then, from God's command are those who, though God ordered them to renounce their wealth while living, want to go on possessing it even after death through their relatives! How far from that devotion are those who will not disinherit themselves for God's sake, when they are unwilling even to disinherit strangers for their own sake! To them I would gladly and freely say: What madness is this, you most wretched people? To make anyone else your heirs, you disinherit yourselves of what is your own. To leave others rich, even for a short time, you condemn yourselves to eternal beggary.

VI. But perhaps someone asks why God now demands more of Christians through the gospel than he formerly demanded of the Jews through the law. The reason is certain: we now pay more to our Lord because we owe more. The Jews once had the shadow of things, we have the truth. The Jews were servants, we are adopted sons. The Jews received a yoke, we received freedom; the Jews curses, we grace; the Jews the letter that kills, we the Spirit that gives life. To the Jews a servant was sent as teacher, to us the Son. The Jews passed through the sea into the desert; we enter the kingdom through baptism. The Jews ate manna, we eat Christ; the Jews the flesh of birds, we the body of God; the Jews the dew of heaven, we the God of heaven. As the apostle says, though he was in the form of God, he humbled himself even to death, even death on a cross. He was not content, that is, to undergo a simple death for us; he heaped the endurance of the utmost tortures upon his voluntary acceptance of death.

For this alone, then, what can man repay, when Christ spent himself for him through the most bitter of punishments? What worthy return will he make to the Lord for himself, when he owes the very God by whom he was redeemed? This is why the Lord wants us to be more devoted to him: he purchased our devotion at so great a price. And so the most blessed Paul says: Who then will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword? The apostle does not say that we owe God money alone or riches alone. We owe him tribulation, distress, famine, the sword, suffering, the shedding of our blood, the breathing out of our soul: in short, a death compounded of every kind of torment. From this let all religious people understand that they do not repay God enough even if they give away all their possessions. Though they distribute everything that is theirs, they still owe themselves.

And therefore, as we had begun to say above, if a woman is a widow, she should not think that the name of widowhood is enough for eternal salvation. Let her see what kind of widow God commands her to be through the apostle, who says: She who is truly a widow, left alone, hopes in the Lord and continues in prayers night and day; for she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives. In one and the same precept the apostle has described two forms of widowhood, one of life and the other of death, and he placed death in pleasures. So he surely does not want a widow to be rich when he does not allow her to live in pleasure, since all the fruit of riches lies in the enjoyment of pleasures. Take away the enjoyment of pleasures, and no reasons for having wealth remain.

VII. Since the apostle has said that death lies in a widow's pleasures, it is plain that he wants everything distributed for the fruit of eternal life, since he wants nothing kept back for the service of death. And therefore he says: She who is truly a widow, left alone, hopes in the Lord. He is teaching that it is not enough for a widow to avoid pleasure and riches unless she clings to God, gives herself to prayer, and is left desolate of all the world's allurements, and by all these things is truly a widow.

If this is so, any woman who wants to belong to life and not to death should by no means think it enough to have renounced pleasures and riches for God's sake, unless by prayer and toil she has also earned the right to be seen as God's widow. For there is no doubt that a person will remain in the body of Christ in the same way that he has clung to Christ in this world, as it is written: My soul has clung to you; your right hand has upheld me. This declares that in the world to come God's right hand will receive only the soul that has clung to God in this world.

This, then, is the rule of widowhood. As for married couples who profess continence and are full of the Spirit of God, who could doubt that people who have banished themselves from the world will not want their goods to serve worldly heirs? How would they hand over what belongs to them to others, when they deny their very selves to themselves? They are endowed with so new a virtue. With the austerity of admirable continence they trample underfoot bodily pleasures that were permitted to them and, what is more, that they had already experienced. How could they fail to vow some of their property to God, when they have made God himself dwell within them? In my judgment, at least, it could quite rightly be said even of such a marriage: Rejoice, barren one, who do not bear; break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor, for the children of the desolate woman are more than those of her who has a husband.

Such a marriage is barren, because it does not bear children. It is desolate, because it has separated itself from all the world's allurements. It is without a husband, because, not making use of a husband, it has a husband in such a way as to seem not to have one. Who, then, would doubt that such spouses, while they live, live for God in their substance as they do in themselves, and when they depart from life, pass over with their wealth to the God for whom they have lived? Otherwise, if any of them leaves his property to people devoted to the world and to the world itself, he has put the name of religion on himself in vain. He appears to have lived all along for the one for whom he dies. So much for married couples.

VIII. Let us pass on to the sacred virgins. The Savior himself laid down the law of devotion for them by the example of the ten virgins. Of these, he says, the foolish girls are to be handed over to everlasting punishment for one reason only: they will lack the work of mercy. By this saying he taught most clearly how highly he valued generous mercy, since he said that without it not even integrity itself would profit a virgin.

But perhaps some of them flatter themselves and think it enough if, while they have large possessions, they give at least a little. I do not refuse to let it be believed, if that is how things really are. Let a little be given, if giving a little will be enough. But I do not know that a little is enough; on the contrary, I know for certain that a little is not enough. If they know otherwise, let them keep that knowledge to themselves. I know one thing: God says that the lamps of the foolish virgins went out because they had no oil of good works.

But you, whoever you are: do you think you have oil in abundance? Those foolish virgins I spoke of surely thought so too. Had they not believed they had it, they would have made sure to get it. For since afterward, as the Lord says, they wanted to borrow it and sought it with all zeal and eagerness, they would no doubt have sought it beforehand too, had they not been deceived by confidence that they had it. So you too, whatever virgin you are, take care that you do not lack it in the same way, even though you believe you have it. You bear the same name as they did and the same profession. You are a virgin, and they too

were virgins. You presume that you are wise, and they did not think themselves foolish. You judge that your lamp has light, and they surely lost their light by presuming on a light still to come. That is why Scripture says they trimmed their lamps: they believed the lamps would be lit. What more? I think some light even shone in them.

For since, as we read, they were afraid their lamps would go out, they certainly had something they feared would be put out. Nor were they wrong to fear it: their lamps did go out, and they were left in darkness. It profited that integrity nothing that the light of virginity was seen in it, for the light failed when the supply of oil ran short. From this we learn that what is too little is as good as nothing. It does little good to light a lamp that will promptly go out. It does not help for something to shine if it sets at the very moment of rising, or to have the beginnings of life only in order to have the beginnings of death.

A full lamp, then, is needed if the light is to last. Even in the lamps that people use for a short time, the light grows faint and fails unless oil is poured in generously. How much oil, then, whoever you are, how great an abundance of oil do you need for your lamp to shine forever? So it is not enough for anyone seeking eternal life to think he has what he does not have. Foolish presumptions lead to perdition, not to salvation: for anyone, says the apostle, who thinks he is something when he is nothing deceives himself.

Unless perhaps, whoever you are, God has revealed to you the measure of generosity, and you have limits for giving laid down by the Holy Spirit. Then you would think it a sin to go beyond them, and judge it a kind of transgression to be more religious than God commands you to be. If that is so, I do not forbid you to use the knowledge the Godhead has granted you. But if this is as false as it is frivolous, what madness it is not to do all you possibly can, out of cautious and fearful foresight, when you have no idea at all what will be required of you for salvation!

IX. It remains to say something about ministers and priests, though some of what is said may perhaps be superfluous. For whatever has been said about all the others applies beyond doubt still more to those who ought to be an example to all, and who certainly ought to surpass the rest in devotion as far as they surpass everyone in dignity. For what is high office without loftiness of merit but a title of honour without substance? Or what is dignity in an unworthy man but an ornament in the mud? And so all who stand high upon the platform of the sacred altar ought to excel as much in merit as in rank.

For if God gave such a rule of life, and one so perfect, to men who are among the laity and to women, weaker by their very sex, how much more perfect does he surely command those to be by whom all are to be taught so that they may become perfect? These are the men whom God willed to be so great an example in all things that he bound them to a singular standard of life by the severity not only of the new law but of the old as well. For although the ancient decree gave everyone ample freedom to increase their wealth, it nevertheless confined all Levites and priests within a fixed limit of possession: it allowed them to have neither grainfield nor vineyard nor any land whatever.

From this one can understand whether our God now wishes his clergy, who live under the gospel, to leave to worldly heirs after them what he did not wish them even to possess while they were still under the law. That is why the Saviour himself in the gospel lays upon them the duty of perfection not as something voluntary, as for others, but as a command. For what do we read that he said to that young layman? “If you wish to be perfect, sell what you have and give to the poor.” But what did he say to his ministers? “Do not possess,” he says, “gold or silver or money in your belts; no bag for the road, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor staff.”

See how great a difference there is between these two sayings of God. To the layman he said, “If you wish, sell what you possess”; but to the minister, “I do not wish you to possess.” And he thought it too little to take from him the possession of larger property unless he also took the very bag away from the apostle who was about to make a long journey, and cut him down to a single tunic. And what next? Not even this is enough. He further commands his servants to travel the world on bare feet, and took the sandals from soles stiff with frost.

What more can be said? He snatched the staff from the apostle's hand, and did not leave his ministers, as they travelled through the whole world, the use of even one little rod. And after this, for their successors, that is, the Levites and priests who carry out so great an administration of divine things, it is too little to be rich themselves unless they also leave rich heirs behind them. Let us blush, I beg you, at this faithlessness. Let it be enough for us that we seem to scorn God right up to the end of our lives: why do we act so as to extend our contempt of him even beyond death?

We have spoken of the persons and offices of each, and all of this for the following reason: as we said above, some who profess religion think either that they do not owe their substance to the Lord as other worldly people do, or at any rate that they owe less, when surely they owe it all the more, because the servant who knows his master's will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows, while the one who does not know it will be beaten with few.

Now religion is the knowledge of God, and therefore every religious person, by the very fact that he follows religion, testifies that he knows the will of God. The profession of religion, then, does not remove the debt but increases it, because to take the name of a religious is to pledge one's devotion; and so a person owes all the more in deed the more he has promised by his profession, according to the saying: “It is better not to vow than, having vowed, not to pay what you promised.”

X. But perhaps someone says: if this is so, then irreligion is safer than religion. Not at all. For the religious person is a debtor because he professes himself religious, and the irreligious person because he has neglected religion; and so each has his debt according to the difference of his condition. The religious person owes whatever he has professed to acknowledge; the irreligious person owes even what he does not deign to acknowledge, according to what the divine word says of him in particular: “He would not understand, so as to do good.”

Yet since we seem to have burdened the religious in this matter by saying that the profession of the name is a pledge of religion, let us remove this burden and suppose that what I said is not so. Let us consider what we ought to do not because of our profession but by reason, not because of a vow but for the sake of our very welfare.

Tell me, I beg you, all you religious: is there any human being who does not do everything he does for the sake either of his salvation or at least of his advantage? No one, I think; for all are led to desire and seek their own advantage by the teaching and impulse of nature itself. So soldiers think their calling honourable, merchants think theirs profitable, and farmers think theirs fruitful. Why say more? Even thieves and robbers, poisoners and assassins, and every kind of wicked way of life think that what they do suits them—not that wicked things suit anyone, but because the one who practises wickedness believes that what is wicked suits him.

So we too, I think, sought the philosophy of religion for no other reason than that we judged it fitting for us. We considered, that is, the brevity of present things and the eternity of things to come, how small the one is and how great the other; we considered also the Judge who is to come and the grave outcome of that dreadful judgement, the burning valley of everlasting tears in the midst of the peoples standing around, a valley which it is an inestimable and supreme evil not only to enter and endure, but even to see and to fear is part of that supreme evil;

we considered too, beside these horrors and torments, those glorious and most blessed things: new heavens and a new earth, a fairer face of all things, the eternal dwelling place of righteousness, the fresh building of creation, golden houses for all the saints above the new-made heavens, halls polished with glittering gems and precious with the gleam of immortal metals, a light there seven times brighter, ever radiant with crimson splendour, a blessedness rich in unspeakable goods, an everlastingness joyful with its inhabitants, the fellowship of the patriarchs, the company of the prophets, the brotherhood of the apostles, the dignity of the martyrs, and in all the saints a likeness to the angels, an abundance of heavenly riches, a flood of immortal delights, a life shared with God.

Thinking on these things, then, and contemplating them, we took refuge in the worship and service of holy religion; we took it to ourselves as a kind of supporter in obtaining these goods and as an advocate of most effective intercession, and with an ambitious humility we placed ourselves under its protection and patronage.

XI. Since, then, we have both considered and sought such great things, let us now look and weigh most carefully whether there is anything in our deeds or our possessions with which we could buy such great things from God. And if there is not, why, I ask, does not each of us offer for himself all that he has, since he cannot offer all that he owes? Especially since our Saviour and God himself has said that nothing is safer or more wholesome for anyone than to devote his property and substance to the service of mercy, and has commanded this above all in both the old and the new law, saying that those who share out what is their own grow richer, and that mercy delivers from death.

And elsewhere, of the holy man: “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever.” In the gospel also: “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth.” And again: “You cannot serve God and mammon.” And again: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation.” And to the greedy and those guilty of the crime of inhumanity he says: “Go into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels.”

What their punishment will be for ever is easily understood, since their lot is assigned with the devil. Yet by those greatest torments it is not the most atrocious crimes of fornication or murder or sacrilege that are punished in them, but solely greed and the inhumanity that renounces mercy.

From this we must understand what those will suffer whom greed has made guilty in addition to other sins, when those who are free of all other sins, but whom the crime of greed alone has condemned to death, are to be subjected to the supreme punishment. If we believe that all these things are to come, we must without doubt avoid them. If we do not avoid them, we certainly do not believe. And if we do not believe, we are by no means Christians; for we cannot call anyone a Christian who does not think that Christ is to be believed.

XII. But suppose that we, though guilty, do not fear the punishments we have spoken of above: can we also hope for a reward we do not deserve? So if we do not give our wealth to redeem our sins, let us at least give it to purchase blessedness; if we do not give so as not to be condemned, let us at least give so as to be rewarded. For even if there are no past evils that the saints need to redeem, there are still everlasting goods which they ought to acquire at a great price; even if there is no punishment to be feared, there is still a kingdom to be sought; and so, even if the saints have nothing to redeem, they still have something to buy. Unless perhaps someone fears a loss in the purchase: that he may lend more than he gets back, that small returns may be paid to one who lends great sums, that the repayment may not match the outlay, that once the great price has been paid the buyer's money may be at risk, and that, if he has entrusted something great to the Lord on earth, Christ may perhaps not have the means to repay him in heaven.

Clearly, if there is this doubt, I advise you to do nothing, since no deeds at all profit one who doubts. Work is empty if faith is not sure; he lends in vain who despairs of being repaid. For Christ, as we believe, is the one who repays all deeds. If, then, you think him either too poor to be able to repay or too faithless to be willing to, how can you hope for repayment from one whom you yourself have condemned for both incapacity and faithlessness?

But if this is not so, and you do not doubt that he will do what he has said, what folly or what error is it not to give him as much as you can, when you surely do not doubt that you will receive much more than you have given? What wretchedness, finally, to prefer to receive nothing of what you leave behind, when you could possess entirely all that you believe in? But—wretch that I am!—I think God is not believed. And as for my saying “I think”: would that I thought it with doubt and did not plainly recognize it! Then perhaps I would labour within myself to overcome my opinions and would force my mind not to believe what was doubtful, so as to turn it to better things.

But what are we to do? We are overcome not by doubtful matters but pressed hard by evident ones. For who believes the Lord with his mind and does not believe him with his means? Who hands over his soul to God and refuses him his money? Who lends faith to heavenly promises and does not act so as to be able to share in what is promised? And so, when we see people not doing these things, we are forced to acknowledge openly and plainly that they do not believe. We cannot think that they put faith in God when they proclaim by their deeds that they refuse it.

Here we must lament and mourn the faithlessness of almost all people. O wretchedness, O perversity! Man believes man and does not believe God; hope is lent to human promises and denied to God. Indeed, everything in human affairs is driven by hope of the future; even this temporal life itself is nourished and sustained only by hope.

This is why we entrust grain to the earth: that we may receive back with interest what we entrusted. This is why the greatest labour is spent on vineyards: because the hope of the vintage consoles people. This is why merchants empty their treasuries in purchases: because they hope to heap them up again through sales. This is why sailors entrust their lives to winds and storms: that they may gain what they hope and pray for. Why say more? Even peace among wild and barbarous nations rests on hope and is confirmed by pledged faith. Even robbers and murderers do not refuse faith to one another, and trust that what they have promised each other will be kept. In short, as I have said, everything among human beings is done in hope. God alone is despaired of; and though our Lord has made the elements themselves and the nature of the world trustworthy, he alone is disbelieved by almost everyone—he who alone made it possible for all things to be believed.

XIII. But perhaps it may be said at this point that people's use of their property is sometimes a matter not of faithlessness but of necessity, and that religious people do not disbelieve God but keep back what is needed for life and its uses; for many holy people are sometimes prevented from the highest perfection of distributing their wealth by their sex, or their age, or the very weakness of a frail body.

Granted, this may be tolerated; but even if it is tolerated, it must be tolerated on this condition: that, according to the nature of the needs and circumstances, what is sufficient is kept and what is excessive is cut away. “For having food and clothing,” says the apostle, “let us be content with these. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil.” So, as we see, salvation lies in necessities alone, a snare in superfluities; God's grace in moderation, the devil's chain in riches. And what does the apostle add straight away? “Which plunge a person,” he says, “into ruin and destruction.”

So if riches contain ruin within them, let us avoid opulence, lest we fall into ruin. Ample and abundant means are said to bring destruction: ample possessions must be fled, lest deep destruction follow. And therefore, whether sex or age or infirmity requires necessities, they ought to be content with what suffices, so that whatever exceeds temporal use is consumed in religious duty.

But if you, whoever you are, man or woman of holy profession, if you gape after preserving your wealth or piling up your means, it is idle for you to plead infirmity. Can the weaker sex not lead its life in any other way unless it distracts the cares of its mind with the extensive management of a huge estate? Can a consecrated virgin or a widow vowed to chastity not keep the perseverance of her holy profession unimpaired unless they brood over weights of silver and gold and know in their conscience that they possess more wealth than their use as possessors requires?

Or, since quiet is most necessary for this sex and for modesty alike, does some woman perhaps think it impossible to keep her quiet unbroken with the services of only a few attendants, unless the din of a huge household beats upon her ears and the tumultuous clamour of crowds resounding around her deafens her? Surely, for a holy soul that longs for true quiet, too great a commotion is not only something to endure, but even to see it is in a way part of the disquiet; and even if someone wishes to subject such crowds to discipline and silence, she still cannot suppress their unrest and keep her own quiet: so true is it that even correcting the disquiet of others disturbs our own quiet.

What we have said about this sex applies to everyone and suits every age, sex and infirmity alike. So there is no reason for anyone to think that riches are fitting for religion or do it no harm: they are hindrances, not helps; burdens, not supports. For religion is not propped up by the possession and use of wealth but overthrown, according to what the Lord himself says: “The care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word of God, and it becomes unfruitful.” Fittingly and quite beautifully he called riches deceitful; for they are both thought of and called goods, and so they deceive people under the name of present goods, when they are the causes of eternal evils.

XIV. But although this is so, as God himself foretold, let us nevertheless make allowance for the wretchedness and weakness of certain people who think they cannot live at all without great wealth. Very well, you, whoever you are, man or woman of holy name and profession: very well, keep your riches, keep your abundance until the end of this life, provided that at least at the end you bestow it on yourself. Very well, choose to use your property and means in this life, provided that, at least when dying, you do not forget yourself, and remember that your substance must be given back to the worship and honour of him by whose gift you know you received it.

What is asked of all of you, O rich of this world, is humane and even delightful. If it cannot be obtained from each of you that you be willing to be poor in this world, let each of you at least grant himself this: not to be a beggar in eternity. You who so flee from present want, why do you not dread it for ever? Timid in brief things, avoid the long and endless ones. Why do you shudder so at poverty in this life? Why are you terrified? What you fear here is far less.
