If you count temporary scarcity a heavy thing, what, I ask, will that scarcity be which will never end? We are, so to speak, pleading the cause of your own mind and your own wishes. If you do not want to be wholly deprived of the use of your property, act so that you are never deprived of it. What we ask of you is something delightful and pleasurable. You who will not consent to be without riches at all, act so that you may always be rich, according to the saying: “If, then, you delight in thrones and crowns, kings of the people, love wisdom, that you may reign for ever.”

Otherwise, what error or what madness is it that there can be any human being who, having spent his life to the last day amid great wealth—which alone is enough to make him guilty—is not generously and wholesomely mindful of himself even at his final departure, and does not help himself from his own resources even at his sick extremity? (This is especially so since, besides riches, which by themselves accuse their owner according to the saying “Woe to you who are rich,” that same owner does not lack other kinds of sins, which have sprung up in the very bosom and womb of riches as from a natural kindling.) What madness that he does not, at least in his last moments, do this, work at this, and earn this with the whole compass of his possessions: that he not depart guilty, not go on his way guilty, not leave behind a soul to be tortured now and a body to be tortured later?

Who, then, is so faithless or so mad as not to think of these things and not to fear them; who with his substance looks to the interests of others rather than his own, and, utterly bereft of every hope of this life and of every support, loses the one plank to which he could still cling like a shipwrecked man in the middle of the sea—and not only loses it, but throws it away and drives it far from himself, striving in every way to leave himself nothing at all by which, when he is about to perish, he might escape?

XV. Since this is so, tell me, I beg you, all who love Christ: can any people at all be so savage and so cruel towards their enemies as these people are towards themselves? No one, surely, is so fierce or so inhuman as not to stop pursuing his adversaries once they are past hope and dying: these people persecute themselves even as they lie at the point of death.

Or is this not persecution—or can there be any greater—for a man to be disinherited by himself, to be made an exile from all good things and, as it were, driven into exile by himself? And this not in the common or usual way but in a new and most cruel one, namely where the soul itself is sent into exile, where the spirit is disinherited from its own possessions. O how much milder are enemies from outside, enemies of the flesh! They are enemies only of bodies; you are enemies of souls as well.

Compared with your crimes, then, their hatred is a light thing. For whatever does harm in this present world is easy to bear; what is grave, what is deadly, is that which will slay in eternity. And so the Saviour himself says: “Do not fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” Easy to bear, then, is the hatred that harms the body but does not harm the soul, because when the body is harmed the soul is beyond loss, and the blessedness of spirits is not interrupted by the sufferings of the flesh. That, then—that is the inexpiable evil, that is the evil beyond all reckoning, which will condemn the whole person utterly and without end. And so your enemies are milder towards you than you are towards yourselves. For every enmity is dissolved by death: but you act against yourselves in such a way that you do not escape your enmities even after death.
BOOK III.

I. In the two preceding books, O my lady, Church of God, we spoke, as it were, separately to two parts of your children: one that loves the world, and another that displays an outward image of religion. In this book, God willing, we wish to speak to both, as the subject and reason require, addressing now one or the other separately, now both together. It remains for each of them to recognize its own part as the reading goes on, and to receive with love for God whatever we say out of love for God.

In all that we have said so far, we have pointed out that mercy and generosity are the special good of all Christians. We have also shown, with witnesses who are, I think, suitable and many, that these contain above all both the merits of the saints and the remedies of sinners. So I do not suppose anyone expects more, especially since anyone who wants more ought to go to the books of God themselves. They are so full of many great witnesses on this point that the whole of the heavenly scriptures almost amounts to a single testimony.

It remains to say something against the faithless replies that some people commonly put forward as a deadly excuse. Speaking in the gospel, the Savior says that wealth and money are lent to people by the Lord so that what was lent may be paid back with manifold interest. He says to the most avaricious debtor: "You wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I have not scattered. You ought therefore to have given my money to the bankers, and on my return I would have received what is mine with interest. So take the talent from him and give it to the one who has ten talents." And shortly afterward: "And throw the worthless servant into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

This passage can also be applied to something else, but it fits this place and subject too, and not unprofitably. The Savior's bankers are rightly understood as the poor and needy, because money that is given out to such people increases. So whatever is paid out to the needy is without doubt repaid by God with interest. That is why elsewhere the Lord himself commands more plainly that the rich should distribute the wealth of the world and make for themselves purses that do not grow old. And through his chosen vessel he also shows that riches are given to the wealthy by the Lord so that they may grow rich in good works.

And so I too, the least and most unworthy of God's servants, say this. The first and most salutary duty of religion is for a rich Christian to spend the riches of this world for the name and honor of God while he is still in this life. The second is that if perhaps he has not done so, held back by fear or weakness or some necessity, he should at least give everything away when he is dying.

II. But perhaps someone says: "I have children." On this point the pages of the first book have already said a good deal that is, I think, to the purpose, and the Lord's word is quite enough on the matter: "Whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me." There is also the saying of the prophet that fathers are not to be judged for their sons, nor sons for their parents, but that each person is either to be saved by his own righteousness or to perish by his own iniquity. Therefore, however much wealth a man heaps up for his children, it will in no way help him at the judgment that he left a rich heir.

But suppose parents can be pardoned if they leave some part of their inherited property to their children, provided the children are good and holy. Suppose too that they can be pardoned if they leave something even to bad and vicious ones. Those who speak like this seem to have some show of an excuse: "Family love won; the force of blood compelled us; nature herself dragged us into her power as if by the hand of love. We knew what God's justice required and what sacred truth demanded, but we were overcome, we confess, by the yoke of fleshly kinship, and we gave our captive hands to the chains of affection. Faith gave way to blood, and the claims of family duty overcame the devotion of religion."

Something can be said, though it cannot be said to one's salvation. It is the shadow of a paltry excuse that does not excuse. It gives the guilty the look of a plea, not freedom from guilt. For I by no means promise anyone that a person who has loved anything more than God can find firm support in anything at all. As it is written, the judgment will consist in this: that light has come into this world, and people loved darkness rather than light. No one doubts that whatever a person has preferred to the love of God will all turn to darkness for him. That, then, is how things stand.

But suppose, as I said, that indulgence can be shown to parents who unwisely indulge nature. What about those who have no children, yet still turn themselves entirely away from any concern for their own salvation and the remedy of their sins? Though they have no offspring of their own blood, they still look for others, whoever they may be, to whom they can make over the substance of their property. That is, they look for people on whom to write some shadowy name of kinship, whom they, as imaginary parents, can make their adopted children, so to speak. Faithlessness begets these heirs to take the place of children who do not exist.

And so these most wretched and impious people, though they are not bound by the chains of children, make chains for themselves with which to bind the unhappy necks of their own souls. Though no pressure of danger exists at home, they summon danger from outside, and though there is no cause for peril, they rush, as it were, into a destruction of their own choosing. Some may find it almost uncertain how to feel about their most unhappy errors: whether to be angry at them or to grieve over them.

For error deserves grief, and impiety deserves cursing. Their misfortune moves us to tears, their faithlessness to anger. In the one case there is reason to mourn human folly, in the other reason to be roused for the love of God. Can any person at all be found, or even exist, who has run the short course of this unhappy life and is now hanging at its very edge, about to go at once to the tribunal of God, yet thinks of something other than his end, other than his departure, other than his danger? Can anyone neglect his hope and his soul, which he ought to help at least somewhat in his last moments with all his zeal, all his effort, all his means and substance, and instead think of this alone and turn this alone over in his mind: how lavishly his heir will eat up his property!

III. Most wretched of all, why are you anxious? Why do you fret? Why do you make yourself the provider of perishing things? Are you perhaps afraid that when you are dead there will be no one to devour what you leave? I do not want you to fear; I do not want you to worry. Would that you could be saved as easily as all your possessions will perish! O faithlessness! O perversity! Even the common saying holds that everyone wishes better for himself than for another. This is a new kind of monstrosity: that someone should wish to provide for anyone at all except himself.

See, most unhappy of all, you are about to go to the sacred examination, to that dreadful and unbearable judgment. There the soul, a stranger and full of anxiety, can have no comfort at all except a good conscience alone, an innocent life alone, or mercy, which comes nearest to a good life. There a guilty man has no help except a generous mind, fruitful penitence, and abundant almsgiving, which are like strong hands. There, finally, according to the difference in merits, you will find either the highest good or the highest evil: either an immortal reward or torment without end.

And you are thinking about enriching your heirs, whoever they may be. You sigh over the wealth of your relatives on your father's and mother's side, and over which of them in particular you should make richer with your patrimony. You think about whom to make over your fine furnishings to, whose storerooms to fill with your stores, to whom to leave the larger number of your slaves. Most unhappy of all, you think how well others will live after you; you do not think how badly you yourself will die. Tell me, I beg you, O wretched, O faithless man!

You divide your patrimony among many and enrich many with your property. Have you then deserved so badly of yourself alone that you do not make a place for yourself as an heir, even among strangers? Look, the officers of the sacred tribunal are already waiting for you as you are about to leave this life. The torturing angels and the terrible ministers of immortal torments are waiting. And you turn over in your mind the pleasures your worldly heirs will have after you; you dwell on the delights of others. You think, of course, how well your heir will dine on your goods after you, with what plenty he will fill his belly, how he will stretch his glutted insides until they overflow to the point of nausea.

Most unhappy of all, what have you to do with these trifles, with these ravings, with the folly of this error, with the ruin of this vanity? Will it be able to help you amid the greatest torments if the man who prodigally eats up your property belches heartily, sleek and well fed?

IV. On the matters we are now discussing, we will add something more later if the subject and reason require it. Meanwhile I say this specifically and urge it with a special warning: let no one at all prefer any loved one, however dear, to his own soul. It is not unjust for any Christian to heap up less in this world even for his lawful heirs, so long as he helps himself in many ways for eternity. It is easier for children to lack something here than for parents to lack something in the life to come, and present scarcity is much lighter than eternal poverty. This is especially so because there not only poverty but also death and punishment are to be feared, so it is surely easier for heirs to lack some of the patrimony here than for testators to lack salvation there. And the very people to whom the inheritance is left should particularly want this, if they have any devotion in them, so that those who leave it may not perish. If they do not want it, they are much less worthy to have anything left to them. For a wise testator is not unjust when he does not leave what an impious heir does not deserve.

Therefore it is best for each person to look out for himself and leave everything to his own soul and salvation. Yet sometimes there are not only children, to whom more seems naturally owed, but also other loved ones whose merit or circumstances are such that justice itself and the worship of God support giving and bestowing something on them. To such people it is not only pious to leave something, but even irreligious not to:

for example, if one's parents are in distress, or one's brothers and sisters are faithful, or one's wife is holy, or, to extend the duty of family love further, if one's relatives are poor, or one's in-laws are needy, or finally if those of any kinship at all are in want, or certainly, what is above all, if they are dedicated to God. For this is the chief and surpassing thing: when what someone does from the duty of family love, he does from the affection of religion.

For blessed is he who loves his own in the spirit of divine love, whose affection is an act of worship of Christ, who in the bond of nature thinks of God, the Father of all natures. Turning the gifts of love into sacrifices, he gains for himself so much immortal profit and blessed fruit that what he bestows on his loved ones he lends to his Lord. By the very act of giving temporary generosity to his own, he earns an everlasting reward for himself.

But now, quite the opposite and most impiously, people leave less to none of their own than to those to whom more is owed out of reverence for God. Family love pays least regard to those whom religion especially commends. Indeed, if parents offer any of their children to God, those who are offered are placed after all the other children. They are judged unworthy of inheritance because they were found worthy of consecration. And so for this one reason alone they become cheap in their parents' eyes: because they have begun to be precious to God. From this one can see that almost no one is held cheaper among people than God. It is surely out of contempt for him that parents particularly scorn those children who have begun to belong to God.

V. But, of course, those who do this give a splendid account of their reasoning. They say: "What need is there to leave an equal share of the inheritance to children who are now in religious life?" So nothing is more just, nothing more fitting, than that because they have begun to be religious, they should beg! It is not that being cut off from earthly property will crush them with beggary. They possess heaven in hope and will soon possess it in reality as well, ruled and protected by their God, who rewards them both with the immortal hope of eternal things and with enough of the things of time. Still, as far as the inhumanity of their parents is concerned, they are in want, since they were left in such a way as to be in want. Certainly there are some who are not thrown out of the house altogether, and who are not wholly denied fire and water like exiles. Even so, they are left so far below their brothers that, even if they do not suffer actual poverty, they seem to be in want by comparison.

You ask what need religious people have of a fair share of the patrimony. I answer: so that they may carry out the duty of religion, so that religion may be enriched by the property of the religious, so that they may give, so that they may bestow, so that while they have, all who have not may have. Indeed, if their faith and perfection are so great that having, they will soon not have, they will surely be more blessed in not having after they have had.

Why, I ask you, most inhuman parents, do you impose on them the necessity of a poverty they have done nothing to deserve? Leave this to religion itself, to which you handed over your children: it is more fitting for them to make themselves poor. If you are so eager for them to be needy, leave that to their own devotion. Let them be allowed, we beg you, to choose to become poor. They ought to choose poverty, not have it forced on them. And finally, even if they endure it, let them bear it out of devotion, not suffer it as a sentence.

Why do you expel them, as it were, from nature, and disinherit them, as it were, from the right of blood? I too do not want them to be poor, except so that poverty itself may have its reward, and by a glorious exchange they may choose want out of abundance, so that by choosing want they may gain abundance. Yet why do I strive to draw you toward humanity and family love through the very duty of most holy reason, when that is exactly what stands most in the way? The very thing that ought to make parents pious makes them impious.

You ought to leave more of your patrimony to your religious children precisely so that at least something of your property might reach God through them. Instead, you do not leave it to your children precisely so that they will have nothing to leave to God. By splendid reasoning and caution, no doubt, you are content not to acknowledge your children, so that they may not recognize themselves as children of God. What a magnificent return you make for sacred benefits! You take the greatest care that the honor of God may not obtain anything even through your own family, when everything you have is God's gift. Why, I ask, so faithlessly? Why so impiously?

We do not demand that you give what is yours to the Lord: give back to God something of his own. Why do you act so greedily, so impiously? What you refuse is not yours. Do you think it unjust, then, to make your religious children equal in property to your worldly ones? Then you are acting so that those whom religion has made cheap in your eyes may come to regret the religious life they have begun. The Lord, therefore, kind and good, who [?] in them their purpose and profession [?]. But as far as it lies with you, you are acting to make worshipers of the world out of those to whom you prefer your worldly children. For what else is it to hold people in contempt because of religion than to forbid religion?

VI. But perhaps we may seem unjust in accusing all parents equally in this matter, since not all treat their children with equal injustice. "For there are," someone says, "there are many parents who make equal shares for their children. They distinguish them by only one condition: in the shares that seem to be assigned to the religious children, they direct that the use belongs to them, but the ownership to others."

But this is much worse and more faithless. It seems a more tolerable impiety for someone to leave his children less with full ownership than to take ownership of the property from them entirely. Such a condition can be put up with to some extent if something is left on these terms to friends or in-laws or relatives. But a man who does not grant his children ownership of the property leaves them nothing. Yet the utterly unjust faithlessness of parents has found a way to shut God out of their patrimony entirely, by taking ownership of the property away from their religious children. It gave them the use, so that they would have something to live on. It took away the ownership, so that they would have nothing to leave to God.

O new device of an irreligious mind! It has found a way to seem to provide for its children through its greater impiety toward God. It has arranged that the holy offspring, having the use of the property but not the title to it, should live like the rich but die like beggars. In this way the most faithless testator could leave this world in complete security, knowing that nothing at all of his could reach God. And yet I said above that through the use of the property the religious children possess some semblance of wealth. Not even this is true. Even if use seems to amount to something, in their own minds it does not. No one can believe himself rich even for a short while when he knows he owns nothing of his own.

VII. What are you doing, most wretched faithlessness, error of what I might call pagan irreligion? Do you hate God so much that you can stop loving even your own children for this reason alone, that they belong to God? Some people leave their freedmen better off than you leave your children. It is everyday practice for masters to grant Roman freedom to slaves whose service was, if not the best, at least not bad. With it they receive ownership of their savings and gain the right to make a will, so that while living they may hand over their property to whomever they wish, and when dying make it over by gift. More than that, they are not forbidden to take out of their masters' house what they had acquired while they were slaves. Sometimes the kindness of a generous patron gives them so much that he subtracts from his own rights what he grants to his freedmen's ownership.

How much better, O most faithless father, whoever you are, how much better those masters treat their freedmen than you treat your children! They give what they give by permanent right, you by temporary right. They grant their freedmen the power to make a will; you take it away from your children. Finally, they give their slaves their freedom, while you, so to speak, consign your children to slavery. For what else is it but consigning them to slavery, when you do not want them to own anything as the freeborn do?

You are following the practice, then, of those masters whose slaves have not served them well. Judging them unworthy of Roman citizenship, they consign them to the yoke of Latin freedom. They allow them to live under the title of freedmen, but they do not want them to own anything when they die. Since such people are denied the power to make a last will, they cannot give away at death even what they have while alive.

In the same way you require your religious children to be, as it were, Latin freedmen: to live as the freeborn and die as slaves. Bound to their brothers' rights as if by the chain of Latin freedom, they may seem to be their own masters while they live, but they die as though placed under their brothers' power. What great crime, I ask, do you think lies in the name of religion, that you do not believe those who are religious to be your children because they have begun to be children of God? How have they become guilty in your eyes of their good will, as if it were a sacrilege, so that you think they should be treated as worse because they wish to be better?

VIII. But you say you do not do this with that intention. That is just as if someone were to say that he does bad things with a good intention and commits a crime of impiety with a pious mind. What good does it do, most inhuman parents, to insist that you dishonor your religious children with a good intention? The facts themselves reject this; the facts refute it. What you say in bare assertions counts for little; your own actions make you witnesses against yourselves. Do you think it unworthy, then, that holy children who please God should be put on a level with children who serve the world? That is true, and you would judge well, if only you applied that judgment justly and the other way round. That is, you should not think wicked children comparable to good ones, or sinners to saints, and those who excel before God in life and merit should likewise surpass the others in your favor and esteem.

For what is more right, what is more just, than that those who are better should also be more honored? Those who win in the judgment should also win in the reward; those who stand first in the sacred gospel should also stand first in a human will. At least in this, the family love and will of parents should agree with the will of Christ, so that the children whom God had preferred by choosing them, the parents too would put first in rank. But not only is this not done; everything is done the opposite way. The defiled are preferred to the pure, the impious to the faithful; darkness is preferred to light, earth to heaven, the world to God. And do such parents think they will escape the judgment of God, even in this one matter, when they trample on the worship of God and the dignity of his judgment by their unworthy conduct?

IX. But of course parents say that they do this not out of contempt for God but for a good reason. For to whom, they ask, are people who have no children to leave the property they leave behind? I will tell you to whom. I will not name those I spoke of above, God's poor, and not strangers or people far away, in case that seems harsh or unkind. I mean people who are dear and inseparable, whom even you who have many offspring rightly put before your children: themselves, I say, you most faithless parents, I say themselves. Can anything be found closer or dearer to anyone than himself? We commend to each of you your own soul, your own salvation, your own hope.

And do you call yourselves devoted because you love your children? Nothing could be called harder than you, nothing more inhuman, nothing so savage, nothing so impious, since no one can get you to love yourselves at all. 'Skin,' says the devil in the sacred Scriptures, 'skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his soul.' Even the devil did not deny that a man's own soul is dearest to him. He strives to turn everyone entirely away from love for their own souls, yet he admits that souls ought to be dearest to all.

What madness is it, then, that you hold cheap your own souls, which even the devil thinks precious? What madness is it that you hold them cheap, when even the one who tries to make them cheap says that they ought to be dear to you? And so whoever neglects his own soul loves himself even less than the devil judges he should. This being so, look, you who think that religious people have no one to leave their property to. Look, even by the devil's opinion, and see whether those who have themselves have no one.

X. I think that what we have already said is quite enough for the part of the matter now under discussion. But perhaps you want this shown to you not only by the force of the facts but also by the authority of examples. I could indeed say that God's commands are greater than all examples. Whether people fulfil them or not adds nothing to the authority of the divine words, since their force certainly rests on the person of the Lord and not on the obedience of his servants. Nothing can be added to them or taken from them by us, for their honor is always the same, because God is their author.

Still, human weakness may wish to be helped by human examples as well, so that it can more readily do now what it learns others have done before. We showed in the first book that the things which some imitators of Christ still do today were once done not sparingly but abundantly, not by a very few but by whole peoples, and not in the most ancient times but almost very recently. For what do the Acts of the Apostles tell us, which are new and still almost before our eyes? 'All who believed,' it says, 'were together and had all things in common.' And again: 'Great grace was upon them all; for there was no one in need among them. For all who owned lands or houses sold them, brought the price of what was sold, and laid it at the apostles' feet.' And elsewhere: 'No one said that anything he possessed was his own.'

And this was no small number of believers, which needs saying in case the authority of Scripture moves someone less because he thinks these are the examples of only a few. How great the multitude of the first church was can be seen from this alone: right at the very beginning eight thousand men are reported to have joined the church in two days. From this one may estimate how large a multitude of every kind grew up over the other days, when just two days produced so many men, not counting people of other ages and of the other sex.

Since that people was already so countless and so perfect, I ask all you parents to whom I am speaking: among those many thousands of believers, who lived with such perfect faith, did all of them have children, or did none of them? Neither, I think, for every congregation of the church is a mixture of both. So those Christians who have no children can understand to whom they ought to leave their property when they see to whom the childless left theirs back then. And if they do have children, let them learn what they too should do when they see that parents then put the love of God before their children.

Every age, then, and every condition has something to follow. Whoever shares in the faith should make himself a sharer in that blessed example. If those people, giving everything they had for God's sake, disinherited even themselves while they were alive, learn, we beg you, at least to make yourselves the heirs of your own goods when you die. Believe me, even among your children you must not forget your own salvation and your souls. That your children are close to you and very closely bound to you is certain enough. But believe me, no one is closer to you, no one more bound to you, than you yourselves. So love them (we do not object), love your children, but in second place after yourselves. Love them in such a way that you do not seem to hate yourselves, for a love that is mindful of another and unmindful of itself is ill-advised and foolish. 'The son,' says sacred Scripture, 'shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of his son.' And the apostle says: 'Each one shall carry his own burden.'

XI. So riches left to children do not free parents from beggary. On the contrary, wealth left to children without measure is the parents' everlasting beggary, and so no one does parents more harm than children who are loved too much. For while the children abound in their father's goods, the parents are tormented for eternity. Even if a son is so devoted that he later wants to share the goods left to him with his father in order to cool his father's punishment, he will not be able to. After death, a son's devotion cannot give back to a father what each person's own lack of devotion and lack of faith has denied him.

And so, as the apostle says, let each one think of his own load, since every man will carry his own burdens. The flames of the unhappy dead are not cooled by the riches of their heirs. That rich man in the Gospel who was clothed in purple and fine linen had no doubt been wealthy in this world, and by his death he had also made his heirs rich. But it did him no good at all that his rich brothers sat brooding over his wealth and talents while he could not get a single drop of relief. They lived in abundance, he in want; they in rejoicing, he in pain; they in riches, he in torments; they perhaps forever in luxury, he forever in flame.

O unhappy and pitiable condition! With his goods he had prepared happiness for others and affliction for himself, joys for others and tears for himself, a brief pleasure for others and everlasting fire for himself. Where were his in-laws then, where his kin, where his sons, if he had any, or his brothers? He remembered them, and he had surely loved them so much that he did not forget them even when he was placed in punishment. What good were they to him? What help did they give him?

The unhappy man was tormented, and while others devoured his wealth, he burned and begged for a drop of relief and could not get it. And, as if anything could be added to his punishment, he asked that it be given him by the very man he had once despised: the man who had rotted in pus and gore, whose stench and filth he had shunned from afar, who had fed dogs with the sores on his limbs, and whose wasted body swarming masses of worms had furrowed to its very depths. O condition grievous beyond measure, and worthy of mourning!

The poor man bought blessedness with beggary; the rich man bought punishment with his wealth. The poor man, though he had absolutely nothing, bought eternal riches with his want. Oh, how much more easily the rich man could have acquired them with all his possessions! Burning amid torments and crying out amid punishments, he said: 'Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.' Then, of course, that rich man did not shudder at the hand of Lazarus, once a poor man, nor did he scorn his help. He begged that Lazarus' fingers be put into his mouth, and that the unbearable flames in his throat be soothed by the service of that hand, once foul and filthy. Oh, what a reversal had taken place! He now longed to be touched by the man he had once scorned even to look at.

XII. So let the rich think about these things, those who are unwilling to redeem themselves with their wealth so as not to suffer them. The man we are now speaking of was rich, and the people we are now speaking to are rich too. They share one name; let them beware that they do not also share one condition. Rich sons will not free guilty parents, and a wealthy heir overflowing with luxuries will not quench the flames of the wretched testator. It is hard for someone to leave little to his children and his kin;

it is far harder to be tormented for eternity. For I think that while that rich man was being tormented, he was not so much delighted by his heir's wealth as pained by the torments of his own body. He was not so much delighted that his heir was feasting well as pained that he himself was cruelly tormented; not so much delighted that his heir was awash in exquisite luxuries as pained that he himself was wasting away in unbearable fires; not so much delighted that his heir was feeding parasites and gluttons from his wealth as pained that he himself was feeding the flames with his own marrow.

And I think that if anyone had then offered him the choice between having rich heirs and not being in misery and torment himself, he would certainly have wanted them stripped of all their goods, if only he could be freed from all his evils. He would have wanted to offer everything he had owned, if only he could escape what he was enduring. He would have wanted to give, for his own sake, all the property he had had, all his temporal treasures of silver and gold, so that, if he somehow could, he might heap the mass of his riches upon the unceasing torture of undying punishments and quench that everlasting fire, and might hold back the overflowing balls of flame by setting against them the immensity of his vast wealth.

But why do I say that he would have wanted to redeem that endless evil with his wealth? I say something more: he would have wanted to hand over all his property if he could buy himself, as he lay in the flames, rest for even a single hour. He longed for even a poor man's finger dipped in water to soothe the flames in his throat; how would he not have preferred to buy rest at any price, when he begged so earnestly for one small drop of relief?

But what good was any of this then? How did it help the wretched man that he now wanted to offer everything for his own sake, when before he had wickedly refused? Or what good was it then that he longed to give everything, which he had already lost, when he had given nothing for his own sake while he possessed everything? For late, as the Holy Spirit says in the Scriptures, late is the repentance of the dead. How so? 'For there is no one in death,' the divine word says to God the Father, 'who remembers you; and in hell who will confess to you?'

Scripture declares that the dead sinner is shut out entirely from confessing his sin, and that no one who forgot God in this life can remember him afterward. So completely is all hope cut off from him and every way to life barred that, although the guilty have one way to salvation, namely to pour out prayers to God and beg unceasingly for heaven's mercy, the sinner is condemned even here by the penalty of a deadly forgetfulness, so that he is not left even the memory of God, from whom he ought to hope for salvation.

Let them think about this, then, those who want their children to be rich after their death and do not remember the punishments to come even when they are dying. Let them think about this, those who condemn themselves to eternal death so as to have rich heirs in this fleeting and brief life. In this they do not so much love their heirs as hate themselves, because a love that looks to a brief advantage is not as wholesome as a hatred that will torment for eternity is grievous. And that is why our God, as we said earlier in the first book, commands parents to store up discipline for their children, not money, and tells them to bestow what lasts forever, not what perishes. This is because such things and holy work benefit children and parents alike: the children through instruction in discipline, the parents through generous giving. For discipline gives children everlasting salvation, and generosity lets parents escape everlasting death.

XIII. But to whom am I saying these things, or why am I saying them? Where shall we find open ears or seeing eyes? For all, as we read of the ungodly, almost all have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is no one who does good, hardly a single one. A new madness has seized people, both worldly people and some who profess religion. As we had begun to say earlier, they now make over their own property, that is, the price of their own redemption, not only to children or grandchildren, which can be tolerated because of the bond of nature, but also to relatives on the father's side and on the mother's side; and not only, as they say, in the direct line, but also in the oblique and collateral lines, or rather to people coming from a line that is averse and perverse.

And it hardly matters to people any more whom they provide for, so long as they do not provide for themselves at all. If any of the people we are speaking of have no children as death approaches, they most faithlessly look for people to call their relatives or in-laws, or, if there are none, they at least look for some made-up names of new kinships. As I said, it does not matter to them whom they remember, so long as they forget themselves. It does not matter whom they claim to love, so long as they hate their own souls, and it does not matter whom they make rich, so long as they waste themselves away in eternal beggary.

XIV. O misfortune, O insanity! What, I ask, have these most wretched of all men done so badly against themselves that, while serving the pleasures of others, they persecute themselves forever? You can see some people, with the most unhappy vanity, hunting out new and noble relatives. You can see the shameful names of unknown kinships and the ridiculous fabrications of recent and very powerful family ties, when someone says of some adopted and sudden relative: 'I make so-and-so, my kinsman, my heir'; or some widow or virgin of holy profession says: 'I name so-and-so, my next of kin, as my heir.' And so some people suddenly, at the very end, have as relatives those whom they had treated as outsiders and strangers all their lives, and people who were always strangers to the living begin to be the kin of the dead.

They suddenly bring into their wills people they never brought into their affections, and especially, as I said, the wealthy, the noble, or the high-ranking, people who would perhaps not have been relatives at all if they had not been powerful. How ridiculous the ambition of the wretched testator! He gives the value of his own property to purchase a false kinship and buys the name of an heir with the price of the inheritance. With all the strength of his patrimony he labors so that the one written down as heir will not deny that he is his relative, and so that the most unhappy testator, by the most foolish and wretched vanity, having made a noble his heir, may seem more honored in death after seeming humbler in life. O blindness, O insanity!

With how much effort, you most unhappy people, you bring it about that you will be wretched for eternity! With how much less care and striving you could have made sure that you would be blessed forever! I can find no other cause for this at all except unbelief and faithlessness alone: that is, people either do not think they will be judged by God or do not believe at all that they will rise again. For no one who is certain that he will rise again and be judged by God for his good and evil works would fail to serve either his hope and blessedness, so as to receive everlasting goods for his good deeds, or his fear and peril, so as not to suffer eternal evils for his evil deeds.

XV. But presumably it seems abhorrent to the Christian name for anyone to be said not to believe in the things to come. Then what reason is there that, if a man believes what God has said, he does not fear what God threatens? And, if he does not believe the words God has spoken, that he does not believe the rewards God promises? For no one proves that he believes God's promises if he does not act so as to be able to reach the rewards God has promised.

In this very life, if someone learns that he is to be judged by human authority and dragged before an earthly tribunal, he looks for advocates, engages patrons, and buys the goodwill and favor of officials. He does all this out of fear of the coming trial, even though he cannot purchase the outcome of the trial. So, even if he cannot buy victory itself, he still pays dearly for the hope of victory.

Tell me, whoever you are who say that you believe in God's judgment: if you believed, even after the example of the people I just mentioned, that you would be judged by God, would you not purchase your hope and salvation at any price? But you certainly do not believe. You do not believe, and though you want to assert your belief in words, you do not believe; for, as the apostle says, you confess in words but deny in deeds.

Finally, to prove your unbelief to you by your own conduct, tell me, I beg you, whoever you are who leave your property to some rich relative or in-law, or, if there are none, even to a stranger: why did you not give it up while you were healthy and unharmed? Why did you not hand it over to your heirs while you were well and vigorous? Why instead do you stipulate most providently in the will itself, and write carefully and diligently: 'When I have departed from human affairs, then you, so-and-so, my dearest, shall be my heir'?

Tell me, please, why you give nothing of yours to this person who, as you say yourself, is dearest and most closely bound to you, and hand over nothing of yours for as long as you think you will live, but only when you see that you are going to die? And why do I say 'when you see that you are going to die'? On the contrary, you take the most provident care that he should have nothing of yours while you are still breathing or even while you are dying, but only when you are completely dead and gone. And it is a wonder that you even allow him to have your things once your funeral has been held, and not only after you have been carried out and buried. Though even this you seem to have guarded against when you say, 'when I have departed from human affairs.' For to depart entirely from human affairs is for the whole man, body and all, to have ceased altogether to be present among human affairs.

So tell me, why do you stipulate these things so providently in your will? Why do you insert them so anxiously and prudently? No doubt because you judge that your property is necessary to you while you live, because you do not want to be parted from your wealth, and because you think it most unjust that while you are alive and well someone else should become rich on what is yours while you waste away in beggary. That is true. I do not reject this concern as unreasonable, and I approve whatever you say along these lines. But on one point I want you to satisfy me.

How is it that you, who think the use of your goods so very necessary for yourself, do not think the fruits and revenues of your property necessary after death? No doubt you say: 'A dead man needs nothing, and nothing has to be kept for me for that time, since once I am dead and feel nothing I can neither be delighted by possessing my goods nor tormented by losing them.'

The reason is plain. So when you are dying you assign your property to someone else because you yourself cannot reap its fruits after death. But what of the fact that the apostle Paul, God's chosen vessel, testifies and cries out that whatever a man sows in this life he will reap after death, and that 'he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessing will also reap from blessing'? By this he plainly meant us to understand that those who sow stingily cannot reap blessing. For when he said, 'he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessing will also reap from blessing,' he clearly placed blessing in generosity alone, and so he showed that stingy sowers will reap beggary and generous sowers will reap blessing.

XVI. But perhaps these things seem to you, whatever unbeliever you are, either not strong enough or not clear enough. What, then, of the fact that the Lord himself in the Gospel teaches most plainly that a Christian loses nothing of his good works? He says: 'Whoever gives one of these least ones a cup of cold water to drink, only in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward.' What could be said more clearly? He said that even something with no value in the present will have a reward in the future. He gave such honor to service done for him that something which is utterly worthless here because of its cheapness would count for something there through faith.

But in case some people flattered themselves on this point, thinking that because they have much they could buy great things with little, he was careful to say that even for a cup of cold water the reward will not be lost. In this way he clearly showed, not that something great will be paid back for something small, but that no work of faith whatever will be lost.

So you have an assurance beyond doubt of a future reward; you have a fully adequate surety that good works will be repaid. He is so faithful, and so merciful and kind as well, that he does not merely pay what he has promised as though it were a debt, but also shows a way to make himself a debtor. For when he said he would give a reward for a cup of cold water, he not only wishes to repay what he has received but also points out things for which he will pay. Kind as he is and full of mercy, and wishing to provide not only for the generosity of the rich but also for the humble service of the poor, he showed how even someone with nothing at all to lend could in some way make God his debtor.

XVII. But perhaps you, whoever you are who are rich, think this work of the poor unworthy of your means, and wish to hear some pledge of the sacred promise that belongs to you in particular. You have, first, what God says to the rich man in the Gospel: Go, sell all your goods, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then there is what he commands for everyone in a prohibition: Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, but store up

for yourselves treasures in heaven. Finally there are the words by which he invites all who own the things of this world to the work of overflowing generosity, with the hope of a boundless reward. He says that everyone who, for the sake of his honour and love, spends a house or a field or any other property on works of mercy will receive a hundredfold in the future: and besides that, he says, he will possess eternal life. What greater pledge could he give to those who believe him than to promise that he will repay a hundredfold to those who lend to him lavishly?

And not only this: he will possess eternal life, he says. This is far more than the hundredfold repayment itself, because whatever someone has received a hundredfold he will possess forever. Then it will not be a fragile and perishable possession, nor will it vanish like earthly riches, as a passing shadow or a fading dream. Whatever God has given will be immortal; whatever has been received will last without end. And so, as I have said, whoever receives in this way receives more than a hundredfold, because the fact that the hundredfold itself is everlasting surpasses the value of a hundredfold.

XVIII. Since this is so, and since whoever believes in God will without doubt receive such great things, how can you think that after death you will not enjoy the things you have given to God, when the Lord promises you not only their use but their increase as well, and an overflowing abundance? Or perhaps you do not want to receive such great things? But reason does not allow you not to want them.

For there is no one among human beings who, when he could be blessed, prefers to be wretched; no one who, when he could have the delights of the highest good, wants to suffer the punishment of the greatest evil. Surely no one, no one at all, and therefore not you either, unless perhaps there is in you some monstrous nature at odds with the human race, so that you alone utterly refuse to be well off, you alone flee from blessedness, you alone delight in punishment.

But if that is certainly not the case, what reason is there why, at least when you are dying and in your last moments, you do not see to it, through the service of a final offering and with the whole range of your property, that you may be rich and blessed if you can earn it from God; or, if you cannot, that you at least are not wretched, at least are not burned, at least are not tortured, at least are not killed off in the outer darkness and roasted in flames that burn without end?

What reason is there, then, as I said, why you do not do this? What reason is there why you do not buy eternal goods? What reason is there why you do not fear eternal evils? What else, surely, but what I said before: either you do not think you will be judged by God, or you do not believe at all that you will rise again? For if you believed it, how could you fail to flee the incalculable evil of the coming judgement and avoid the torments of undying punishment?

But you certainly do not believe; you do not believe. Although you assert otherwise both in speech and in profession, you do not believe. For your speech and your profession boast of faith, but your life and your death proclaim unbelief. Otherwise, prove me wrong: I want to be proved wrong. I do not ask you to prove your belief to me by the deeds of your earlier life: I am content with one piece of evidence, that of your last moments.

See, now, see, you are dying. You are about to leave the house of your body, not knowing where you will go, where you will be led away, to what punishments and to what horrors you will be dragged off. Only one refuge remains to you in your last moments; one glimmer of hope of escaping the eternal fire is given you: that you offer on your own behalf at least what you have in property, since you no longer have anything else you can offer to God. And you, forgetful of yourself and unmindful of your salvation, are thinking about new legatees and sighing over how to enrich your heir.

And while doing this you say that you believe in God's judgement, you who, though you are to be judged, do not look out for yourself even in your last moments? And you claim to believe something about the salvation of your soul, you who hold nothing cheaper than your own soul, and for whom it hardly matters whom you benefit, so long as you harm yourself? And you say that you believe in the judge to come, you for whom no one is lower or more despised than the judge himself? For you scorn him so much, you despise him so much, that you do not even look out for yourself, so long as you can disregard his commands.

Or else refute me and prove me wrong, if I am lying. See, as you are dying, your judge himself, who is going to judge you, cries out to you that in disposing of your goods and property you should not love any person at all more than yourself; that in dying you should not provide for anyone out of your property more than for yourself; that you should consider no one closer to you, no one dearer, than your own soul. For what will it profit a man, says the Saviour, if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?

That is to say: what will it profit you, most unhappy man, if you either have the whole world yourself or leave it to your relatives, if you suffer the loss of your salvation and your soul? For the loss of the soul carries absolutely everything away with it, and a man can have nothing at all who loses himself through the loss of a perishing soul. Or what, he says, will a man give in exchange for his soul? That is to say: do not look to money, man, nor to property, and do not hesitate, at least when you are dying, to offer as much of your goods and means as you can for the sake of your hope. For whatever you give for yourself is cheap; whatever you offer for yourself is of little value, because your soul is more precious than all things put together. And therefore do not hesitate to give for yourself at all, because if you lose yourself, you lose everything in yourself; but if you gain yourself, you will possess everything with yourself and in yourself.

XIX. So, when your Lord cries these things to you as you are dying, whoever you are, you close your mind and stop up your ear. Asserting your faith in bare words, you think words are enough for you in place of deeds, and you consider that you have firm enough support for your belief if you seem to honour with lying words the God whom you despise in your actions and deeds. Son, says holy Scripture, if you have the means, do good to yourself and offer good offerings to God.

And elsewhere it says: Have pity on your soul. See how merciful the Lord our God is, who asks us ourselves to have mercy on our own behalf: Have pity, he says, on your soul. That is to say: you too have pity on the one for whom you see me broken with compassion; have pity at last on the one on whom I always have pity; have pity at least on your own soul, since you see me having pity on one that is not mine. And after this, most wretched man, when God deals with you like this, do you not give in? He asks you to have pity on yourself, and you refuse? He pleads your case before you, and cannot win it from you?

And how, most wretched one, whoever you are, how will he hear you later as you plead in his judgement, when you yourself refused to hear him here as he pleaded for you? But of course there is a weighty reason why you cannot listen to God. For around you in your sickness stand your kinsmen and relatives; around you stand wealthy matrons; around you stand noblemen; a crowd decked out in silk and gold-embroidered garments besieges your sickbed. Oh, what a great fruit for eternity it is to bestow your own goods on such beggars! A worthy reason, no doubt, and quite a just one, that you should take away from your soul what you leave to such needy people!

But no doubt you are overcome with compassion and won over by the devotion of your lamenting relatives. That is certainly a reason. For you see people in the richest and most splendid dress weeping for you, showing you, with gloomy looks and festive clothes, faces composed into sorrow, buying your inheritance with their make-believe concern. Who would not be moved by such devotion? Who would not be moved by such grief? Or how, when you see such things as these, could you fail to forget yourself? For you see forced tears, feigned sighs, pretended anxiety, not hoping that you will recover but waiting for when you will die; you see everyone's eyes fixed on you, as though they were reproaching you for being slow to die.

O unhappy and most wretched man, whose final departure so many relatives long for! Except that I know, and am quite sure, that the prayers of such people carry no weight at all with God. Otherwise I might perhaps wonder that you were still alive, when so many want you to die. And for the sake of these, whoever you are, for the sake of people like these, you abandon your soul, and you say that you believe in God's judgement, when you despise his commands so far as to leave your inheritance to people like this?

He has scattered abroad, says the prophet of the one who believes in God, he has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever. And the Saviour himself says to all the rich: Sell what you possess and give alms. And elsewhere: Sell what you have and give to the poor. Does he say, Give to your kinsmen? Does he say, to your in-laws? Certainly not, but to the poor, to the needy. Does he say to a rich relative, or to any powerful person whatever? Certainly not, but to the destitute, to those in want.

For when you have given your property to your wealthy relatives, does your righteousness endure forever? Or when you have added your riches to theirs, will you have treasure in heaven? Woe, says the prophet, to those who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter. God forbids you even to praise such people, and you are not afraid to make them rich? He does not want words of praise given to them, and you lavish talents on them as well? He forbids their way of life to be honoured with false words, and you pile up their treasures and riches?

XX. But of course you are wary of the looks of the relatives sitting around you, and you fear offending those who are present and besieging your bed. Do not fear them, says the Lord through the prophet, and do not tremble before their faces, for they are a provoking house. So you too must be fearless and steadfast: do not dread their looks or be broken by their pressure.

Despise those who covet your inheritance and are already dividing your property among themselves, who love not you but your estate; indeed, who curse you out of greed for your goods. For while they thirst impatiently for what is yours, they hate you, and judging your presence to be a rival and an adversary to them, they regard the fact that you are alive as a barrier and an obstacle to their greed.

So despise people like this and take no account of them. Do not let their flatteries move you: they are poison to you. Do not heed their fawning: they are swords to cut your throat, and more hideous indeed than an enemy's iron swords. For everyone sees those men, but the unwary do not see these; those, because they rage openly, are avoided, while these, because they lie in wait in secret, kill. And they are all the more dangerous, and worse by reason of a new kind of harm, in that no one at all wishes to be wounded by those iron swords, whereas many even wish to be killed by these. A new and incalculable lure of deadly evil! Whoever is struck by those swords is tormented by fear and pain alike; whoever is killed by these is delighted.

Flee this evil, then; flee the flattery that lies in wait for you; flee the attentions that harm you; flee the solicitations that deceive you. These are the services that cut your throat; these are what drag you to death. Flee the flatteries of such people; flee their eagerness to please: they are your executioners and torturers, who court you now but will kill you in the future, and who, as if hand in hand and banded together in a conspiracy, are trying to drive you and hurl you headlong into the everlasting fires of hell. So do not fear them or be terrified of them: lift up your spirit and take on the strength of holy authority. For if they strive so hard for you to perish, why should you not strive with greater spirit to live? Be strong, then, and look out for yourself with a steadfast spirit. Anyone is faithless enough, and foolish enough, who would rather do others a service and be wretched himself than do himself a service and be blessed, and who, to make others abound in passing delights, hands himself over to be burned in everlasting fires.
Book IV.

I. I am well aware, my lady Church, nurse of blessed hope, that what I said in the earlier books displeases some of your sons who love Christ too little. But I do not set great store by their wishes. It is no wonder that words which speak of God do not please those whom perhaps God himself does not please. Nor should we expect people who do not love salvation itself or their own souls to love a discourse that commends salvation and souls. So in this matter, as in others, the mind and judgment of the saints alone are enough for us. Since they think as we do, we are certain that God himself thinks with us as well. For since the Spirit of God abides in his saints, God is without doubt on the side from which the Spirit of God does not depart.

The opinions of wicked men, then, that is, of pagans or worldly people, should either be valued little or counted as nothing at all; for, says the apostle, if I wished to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ. What is harder and more painful is that some of your sons, I think, dissent from religion while bearing the title of religion, and have left the world in their dress rather than in their minds. Unless I am mistaken, their view holds and asserts that every Christian, without exception, should at the point of death give more thought to his kinsfolk than to Christ.

And because this view was in itself utterly profane and detestable, they try, I think, to veil this most faithless teaching with a kind of shadowy addition. They say that all who believe in God ought to be dutiful to Christ only while they are healthy and well, but that those who are already departing from the world should be mindful of their fleshly kin rather than of their duty to God. As though Christians ought to be one kind of people when well and another when leaving this world; as though everyone should present himself to Christ one way in health and another in death, one way in the earlier part of life and another in the later!

If that is so, then a man will have one Christ when young and another when old, and people must change their faith as often as they change their age. For if someone is to be one person in the worship of God when vigorous and another when weak, one when healthy and another when sick, then God himself will be changeable for man according to the unequal states of the human body, and religion will differ as often as a person's health changes. As though those who ought to belong to Christ when they are well ought not to belong to Christ when they are dying!

And where, then, is that saying: He who perseveres to the end will be saved? Or that oracle of the divine word in the sacred Proverbs: Wisdom is sung at the departure? This surely shows that, although wisdom is wholesome at every age, all people ought above all to be wise at their departure. For the prudence of a past life will not deserve any praise at all unless it is closed by a good end; for wisdom is sung at the departure.

Why did it not say that wisdom is sung in childhood or in youth, in a state of safety or amid the prosperity of good fortune? Clearly because in all these whatever is praised is uncertain. As long as someone is subject to change, he cannot be praised with confidence; and therefore, as it says, wisdom is sung at the departure. For one who departs from the uncertainties of danger, having escaped all the shifts of fortune, will earn a sure verdict, because praise is stable and firm only when the merit of the one praised can no longer be lost. Wisdom, it says, is sung at the departure.

What, I ask, is a Christian's wisdom? What but the fear and love of Christ? For the fear of the Lord, it says, is the beginning of wisdom; and elsewhere it says: perfect love casts out fear. So, as we see, the beginning of wisdom lies in the fear of Christ and its perfection in love. If, then, a Christian's wisdom is the fear and love of the Lord, we are truly wise only if we love God always and above all things. This holds at every time, but especially at our departure, because wisdom is sung at the departure.

II. If, then, wisdom is sung at the departure chiefly for this reason, that God is loved above all things, what madness is it for anyone to say that the healthy must put Christ before fleshly kinship but the dying need not? Why should the healthy prefer him if the dying need not? Or if someone can, without offending religion, put his kinsmen and in-laws before Christ at death, why may he not do so with the same religion earlier too? Or if there is any hour at the end of life in which a person ought to love others more than himself or God, why should he not love them more in his earlier life as well?

And so everything comes undone, vanishes and perishes, and it would follow that no one should hold anyone cheaper than himself, nor anyone lower than God. For if there is any time at which God may rightly be placed after in-laws or kinsfolk, there is no time at which he may rightly be placed before them. But if, as is true, there is no time at all when he ought not to be placed first, there is no time at all when he may rightly be placed after. None at all, and therefore not even at the last; for the prophet says that even a righteous man will perish on the day he goes astray.

So if every error is punished with the ruin of the one who errs, and human life is endangered even by the errors that commonly and ordinarily stain human innocence, what do we suppose will happen when sin is committed against God himself through detestable faithlessness? For if, says the apostle, every disobedience received a just recompense, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? And no one neglects true salvation more than the person who puts anything before God. For since our salvation is God's gift and mercy, what way of obtaining salvation is left to someone who despises God himself, on whose mercy our salvation depends?

Or since God is the judge of the living and the dead, what hope can there be at God's judgment for someone who, even while dying, has scorned in his own judgment the very one by whom he is to be judged as soon as he is dead? And therefore, as divine Scripture says, by the judgment with which he judges he will be judged; that is, by the judgment he passes on God he will himself be judged by God. Nor can he think it unjust if in the future the Lord places him after everyone, when in the present he himself places God after everyone. Nor can he complain if God judges him more damnable than all, since he himself judges God of less value than all.

III. But someone says that he does not do this out of contempt for God or because he thinks him of little worth, but out of love or honor for those he has made his heirs. Let us grant that this is so. Yet almost all other offenders, even the most shameful and criminal, have this excuse ready to hand. Fornicators too may say that they do not fornicate in order to scorn God, but because they are overcome by the heat and weakness of the body. And murderers can declare that they do not shed human blood out of contempt for God, but commit their crimes only out of hatred or greed.

But what good does this excuse do the wicked? It plainly makes no difference what reason a person gives for his sin, since every sin is an injury to the Godhead. Yet let us grant, as I said above, that it is so: that no one hands over his property to another rather than to God out of contempt for God, but that he is drawn to it by honor for his heir, or at any rate compelled by love. But what are we to do, when this very thing proves all the more his neglect and contempt of God?

For whoever you are, if by leaving your property to your heirs or to anyone else you show that you honor and love them, then you certainly show that you neither honor nor love God, to whom you do not leave it. So whatever you say in your own defense tells against you, and your love and honor for others amount to contempt and insult toward God.

For since you leave things to others because you honor them, you certainly do not honor God, to whom you leave nothing. Since you leave much to others because you love them, you surely leave nothing to God because you do not love him. For see: man and God alike stand beside you as you die and make your will. The matter is plain and beyond doubt: the one you chose is the one you preferred. If honor is given to one alone, contempt must be found in the treatment of the other. If the man who is preferred rejoices that you love him, God, who is passed over, must grieve that he is not loved.

But you think, no doubt, that God has no need of human generosity, and so you say: "What need is there for man to give anything to him who himself gave all things to all?" Whether the Lord needs our generosity or not, and in what way he needs it or does not, we shall see presently. Meanwhile, since even you have not dared to deny that he provides all things to all, he is without doubt all the more deserving of our generosity because he was generous to us first. The less equal we are to his benefits, the more rightly we try to respond to them with our dutiful service.

For human nature itself and common custom bind everyone by what is almost a universal law: we owe more gratitude to those from whom we receive some act of generosity, since generosity received constrains us to repay what was given. Before someone has had the use and bounty of another's generosity, he is free and not burdened by the interest owed on benefits; but once people have become debtors, their own conscience compels them all to make a return.

So we owe God all the more because we have received everything from him, and we are all the less able to answer his benefits because, even when we wish to repay what we owe, we repay him from what is his own. For this reason no one has cause to be pleased with himself for his generosity. Just as nothing that a man receives from his Lord is his own, so nothing that he gives back is his own. Therefore the penalty for faithlessness is owed by anyone who has refused God what God lent him, while one who has returned what he received cannot claim credit for generosity.

IV. "But God," you say, "does not need repayment." Nothing could be further from the truth than that he does not need it. He does not need it in view of his power, but he needs it in view of his command; he does not need it in view of his majesty, but he needs it in view of his law. In himself he has no need, but in many people he is in need; he does not seek generosity for himself, but he seeks it for his own. And so he does not need it according to his omnipotence, but he needs it according to his mercy; he does not need it in his deity for his own sake, but he needs it in his compassion for ours. For what does God say to dutiful and generous stewards? Come, you blessed, take possession of the kingdom of my Father, which has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, and other things in the same vein. And lest this should perhaps seem too little for the case we are now discussing, he added the opposite side, saying to the greedy and unbelieving: Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which my Father has prepared for the devil and his angels; for I was hungry and you did not give me food, I was thirsty and you did not give me drink.

Where are those who say that the Lord Jesus Christ has no need of the service of our gifts? See, he tells us that he is hungry and thirsty and cold alike. Let any one of them answer: is he not in need who complains that he is hungry? Is he not in need who declares that he is thirsty? I add something more: Christ is not only in need along with the rest, but in far greater need than the rest.

For among the whole number of the poor, not all share one and the same poverty. There are some who lack clothing but do not lack food; many are in need of shelter but not of clothes; many have no home but do not lack means; there are, in short, some who lack much but not everything. Christ alone lacks whatever anyone in the whole human race lacks. None of his servants is exiled, none is tormented by cold and nakedness, without his shivering too. He alone hungers with all the hungry, he alone thirsts with all the thirsty. And so, as far as his compassion is concerned, he is in greater need than the rest. For every
needy person is in need only for himself and in himself; Christ alone begs in the whole company of all the poor.

And since this is so, what do you say, O man who call yourself a Christian? You see Christ in need, and you leave your means to people who are in no need at all? Christ is poor, and you heap up the wealth of the rich? Christ is hungry, and you provide delicacies for those who are overflowing with plenty? Christ complains that he lacks even water, and you fill the storerooms of drunkards with wine? Christ is worn down by want of everything, and you pile up abundance for the luxurious? Christ promises you eternal rewards for the gifts you give, and you lavish everything on people who will give you nothing in return? Christ sets before you immortal goods for good deeds and eternal evils for evil deeds, and you are neither swayed by heavenly goods nor moved by everlasting evils? And you say you believe in your Lord, when you neither desire his reward nor tremble at his anger?

V. You do not believe, then, as I said in the earlier book; you do not believe. Though you feign religion by your clothing, though you lay claim to faith by your girdle, though you counterfeit holiness with your cloak, you do not believe at all; you do not believe. And I say this to men of this kind and to women alike: they do not believe. However much a woman may put on the garb of a holy name and inscribe on herself the title of sacred religion, if she uses her property to provide for others rather than for herself, she certainly does not believe.

For no one who believes would rather have his means benefit others than himself; no one would be content to buy happiness for others with his own misery; no one would wish to undergo eternal want in order to provide passing delights for others. So whoever uses his patrimony to provide for others rather than for himself does not believe at all that what he gives to God will benefit him. For let any of them tell me why he leaves his means to others. Is it not because he has no doubt that they will benefit the person he leaves them to? That is the reason, without doubt.

Therefore, whoever you are, if you leave things to another because you are sure they will benefit the one you leave them to, then surely, if you believed that whatever you spent on religious gifts would benefit you, you would without doubt set it aside especially for yourself. For since you love yourself more than those to whom you leave it, you would all the more leave it to yourself, if you thought, even with the faintest notion, that it would benefit you.

For you do not hate yourself so much that you do not want to benefit yourself; rather, you do not believe that what you leave to the poor will benefit you. That is why you provide for others rather than for yourself: because you do not believe that a religious work will benefit you. So as you believe, so you will receive. You value the Savior very little, and the Savior will value you not at all. You put Christ after others, and Christ will put you after everyone. To you the Lord is worth less even than men who are lost, and you will be counted among the lowest of those who perish.

VI. But perhaps, as I said before, you flatter yourself on the strength of some religious profession. That makes you all the more a debtor, because by your commitment to holiness you promise greater things; and so you will suffer greater punishment, because you have paid less on your pledge. You promise grand things in appearance and deliver nothing in fact. You are guilty of the crime of forgery; you lie to God in everything. It is not without reason that the sacred word testifies that judgment must begin with the temple of God; for, it says, judgment begins from the house of the Lord.

Elsewhere too it says: And begin with my saints. But let us return to what we were saying. Go, says God to the greedy and unbelieving, go into the eternal fire which my Father has prepared for the devil and his angels. But perhaps you think you will be freed from this evil by certain bodily virtues. You boast, for instance, that you have loved chastity. But remember that those whom the Savior in the Gospel handed over to immortal punishment were not charged with unchastity. You remind us that you have cherished sobriety? Neither are those of whom Scripture speaks punished for the crime of drunkenness. You say you have fasted? Neither was it their luncheons that made them guilty.

But of course you have great reason to be pleased with your abstinence and fasting! You fasted, you lived sparingly and meagerly, not so that after your death you might feed the needy with your means, but so that you might swell the fortune of some heir or other with riches. Great indeed are the fruits of abstinence you reap: you ate less bread so that someone else might have more gold. Your belly shrank through thrift so that the treasure of some person, perhaps a vicious one, might grow.

So when you come to God's judgment, you will be quite entitled to claim credit for your fasting, saying: "I fasted, Lord, and abstained, and for a long time held back from the enjoyment of every delight.
