And the facts prove it: for see, my heirs are now overflowing with what was mine, abounding in the plenty of immense riches."

And to borrow something from the Gospel reading as well, what the Savior said of that rich man you too can say of your heirs: "They are clothed in purple and fine linen and feast splendidly every day; they brood over the talents I buried; they lie upon heaped-up piles of silver and gold; I have also supplied them with the means for every pleasure; they are bloated with the delights I left them.

I abstained for a long time so that they might now get drunk. My frugality is their debauchery. The floors of their overflowing dining rooms swim with wine; they make mud of noble Falernian; their tables and embossed plate are constantly soaked with unmixed wine and are never dry. They wallow in luxury on the coverlets I had made; they fornicate in the silks I left them." And when you have said all this in your own defense, how could you fail to deserve an eternal reward from Christ, seeing that you prepared such an abundance of delights for such saints as these?...

VII. O how much better, whoever you are, how much better and more wholesome it would have been for you to be poor and needy rather than rich! For poverty could have commended you to God, but riches have made you guilty. It would have been more fitting for you to be saved through want than to weigh down both yourself and others through your wealth: yourself, by leaving it wrongly to others; others, because they too hold wrongly, and use most inhumanely, what you left them, and after them leave it wrongly to others.

If, then, whoever you are, you wish to be provided for, if you wish to have eternal life and long to see good days, leave your property to the needy saints; leave it to the lame, leave it to the blind, leave it to the sick. Let your means be food for the wretched, let your wealth be life for the poor, so that their relief may be your reward and their nourishment may restore you. For if they eat of what is yours, you will be filled; if they drink of what is yours, you will quench the heat and burning of your thirst. Their clothing will clothe you, and their warmth in the sun will delight you.

So do not think it a cheap and contemptible thing to leave your property to the wretched and needy: in them you will make Christ your heir. And why do I speak only of Christ's name? You do indeed make Christ your heir, but you yourself will receive the profits of the inheritance. For whatever you leave to Christ, you will possess it all through Christ.

But you, I suppose, judge these things to be trifles and despise them as so many dreams and ravings; for you do not believe that Christ spoke the truth. And the facts prove that you do not believe him at all. For since you do not carry out his commands even at the very end, you either think they are nothing at all or condemn them as false. All the saints have reason to mourn and weep over this: that you and others like you believe no one less than Christ.

If some innkeeper promised you something, you would not refuse to trust his promise. If a huckster or a pickle-seller asked you for a loan, you would not doubt that he would return what you had given. Indeed, goods are sometimes lent even to liars and perjurers, once a bond has been drawn up and a guarantor provided.

Christ has given you both a most trustworthy bond and the best of guarantors: the bond, namely, in the Gospel, and as guarantors his apostles; and if that is too little, his patriarchs, prophets and martyrs, and indeed the whole series of the divine writings. And yet you do not believe him or extend him your trust? Whom, I ask, could you find among men so prodigal and so wretched that you would refuse him credit when backed by so many guarantors? So you give your property to the rich and deny it to the needy, you give it to the luxurious and deny it to the saints, you give it perhaps to some reprobate and deny it to Christ. As you have judged, then, so will you be judged; as you have chosen, so will you receive. You will have no share with Christ, whom you have despised; you will have your share with those whom you preferred.

VIII. But perhaps someone from the ranks of the unbelieving will say that this is not a weighty enough matter either to move God or to drag people into eternal peril. I know, of course, that all the guilty always consider their own guilt pardonable. To thieves thefts are slight faults, to drunkards drunkenness seems harmless, and among the unchaste fornication is no crime; for there is no crime at all so great that it is not made light of in the opinion of the person who commits it.

But if any sinner wishes to know how severely God will judge great crimes, let him learn how the saints punish even slight sins in themselves. They know from God's own words of the examination to come, and through their Lord's words they search out his judgments too; and therefore they are always engaged in God's work, always in compunction, always on the cross. Blessed are they who, while showing mercy to all, never wholly pardon themselves, sparing themselves in nothing but spending themselves entirely on God. They are therefore worthy of reward at the judgment to come, because here they stand continually accused in their own eyes.

And what shall I say of their mercy and generosity, a virtue they treat almost as the first step toward all the others? For many of them make this, as it were, the beginning and the cradle of their conversion: before they cross the threshold of the holy profession, they keep nothing of their own property for themselves. They follow, of course, the saying of our Lord: "Sell all your goods and give to the poor, and come, follow me."

And so, meaning to follow God when he calls, they first sell everything and only then follow. They regard riches as burdens and hindrances, and do not think themselves free to follow until they have first thrown off every encumbrance of fleshly baggage. They are also like people who are moving house and send their belongings to the dwelling they have chosen before they go there themselves. Once they have sent ahead everything that belongs to them, they themselves move, their wealth having gone before them, into a home full and well stocked with immortal goods. They are certain beyond doubt that they will lack nothing afterward, since, as they leave a cheap and contemptible dwelling that is about to collapse at any moment, they have left nothing of theirs there to perish. This, then, is the hope of the saints, this their confidence:

by sending their wealth on so richly ahead, they provide for themselves the enjoyment of the eternal abundance of immortal riches. But you, whoever you are, man or woman, who forget your own soul and salvation and strip yourself of your own few possessions, how will you find stored up and waiting for you in the future what you assign here to people who are not in need, or who even have plenty? How do you believe that God will repay you what you yourself will not entrust to God? In short, how can you want repaid what you will not lend? No one expects to be paid back what he has not lent, and no one is so foolish as to think that what he never put out at interest must be returned to him.

And so you can in no way hope for God to repay you, since by not entrusting anything to God you yourself have refused to let God repay you. So the divine saying is fulfilled in you: "Because you have left your riches to others, or to strangers, your tomb will be your home for ever." So is what the Savior says to someone like you: "Because you are lukewarm, neither hot nor cold, I am about to spit you out of my mouth." And again: "You say, 'I am rich, I have wealth, and I need nothing,' and do you not know that you are wretched and poor and blind and naked?"

So let no one who in his will prefers a human being to God flatter himself on the privilege of his way of life and his profession. Feeling secure brings punishment and ruin on a man; presumptuous hopes are a load of guilt; an absolution claimed for oneself prepares condemnation. Whoever excuses himself before himself accuses himself before God, as it is written: "For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself." Let no one, then, treat his own case lightly: no one escapes with more difficulty than the one who has taken it for granted that he will escape.

IX. Perhaps this seems harsh and severe. Why should it not? For all discipline, as the divine word says, is a matter not of joy but of sorrow. These things are harsh and severe. But what are we to do? We are not allowed to change the nature of things, and the truth cannot be stated otherwise than the very force of truth requires. Some people think these things harsh: I know it, and I am quite certain of it. But what are we to do? There is no way to the kingdom except through hard things. "For narrow," says the Lord, "and strait is the way that leads to life." And the Apostle says: "I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to come that will be revealed in us." He says that all human effort is unworthy to be compared with the glory to come.

And therefore nothing ought to seem harsh or severe to Christians, because however much they offer to Christ for eternal blessedness, what is given is cheap when what is received is so great. Nothing a man pays to God on earth is great when it is set beside what is greatest in heaven. It is hard for the greedy to give away what is theirs. What wonder is that? Whatever is commanded of the unwilling is entirely hard.

Almost every divine word has its rivals. There are as many kinds of opponents as there are kinds of commandments. If the Lord commands generosity among men, the miser is angry; if he demands thrift, the spendthrift curses it. The wicked regard the sacred words as their enemies. Robbers shudder at whatever is written about justice; the proud shudder at whatever is commanded about humility; drunkards are hostile where sobriety is enjoined; the unchaste detest it where chastity is commanded. So either nothing must be said at all, or whatever is said will displease one or another of the people just mentioned. Any wicked man would rather curse the law than amend his mind, would rather hate the commandments than his vices.

Amid all this, what are those to do on whom Christ has laid the duty of speaking? If they keep silent they displease God; if they speak, they displease men. But, as the apostles answered the Jews, it is better to obey God than men. Yet I offer all those to whom the law of God is heavy and burdensome a piece of advice, if they do not refuse to take it, on how the things God commands can become pleasing to them. All who hate the sacred commandment have the cause of their hatred within themselves. All their distaste lies not in the precepts of the law but in their own conduct; the law is good, but their conduct is bad. Therefore let people change their purpose and their inclinations. If they make their conduct worthy of approval, nothing that the good law commands will displease them. For once someone has begun to be good, he cannot help loving the law of God, because the holy law of God holds within itself what holy people hold in their conduct. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.
